On the Correspondence between Nested Calculi and Semantic Systems for Intuitionistic Logics
Tim Lyon

Abstract
This paper studies the relationship between labelled and nested calculi for propositional intuitionistic logic, first-order intuitionistic logic with non-constant domains, and first-order intuitionistic logic with constant domains. It is shown that Fitting’s nested calculi naturally arise from their corresponding labelled calculi—for each of the aforementioned logics—via the elimination of structural rules in labelled derivations. The translational correspondence between the two types of systems is leveraged to show that the nested calculi inherit proof-theoretic properties from their associated labelled calculi, such as completeness, invertibility of rules, and cut-admissibility. Since labelled calculi are easily obtained via a logic’s semantics, the method presented in this paper can be seen as one whereby refined versions of labelled calculi (containing nested calculi as fragments) with favorable properties are derived directly from a logic’s semantics.

†
institute:
Institut für Logic and Computation, Technische Universität Wien, 1040 Wien, Austria

Introduction

In his seminal work
Gen35
, Gentzen introduced the
sequent calculus
framework for classical and intuitionistic logic, and proved the celebrated
Hauptsatz
, i.e.
cut-elimination theorem
, for the systems. As a corollary of his theorem, it can be observed that any formula provable in one of Gentzen’s systems, is provable with an
analytic derivation
, that is, a derivation where all formulae used to
reach
the conclusion of the derivation,
occur
in the conclusion of the derivation. This method of proof happens to be of practical consequence, and as such, many variations and extensions of Gentzen’s sequent calculi have been assembled and proposed—examples include tableaux calculi
Fit72
;
Fit14
, display calculi
Bel82
;
LyoIttEckGra17
;
Wan94
, hypersequent calculi
Avr96
;
Pog08
, labelled calculi
Gab96
;
Sim94
;
Vig00
, and nested calculi
Bru09
;
Bul92
;
Kas94
. Such calculi have been applied to provide decision algorithms
Gen35
;
Pog08
, to automate the extraction of interpolants
LyoTiuGorClo20
, and to automated counter-model extraction
LyoBer19
;
TiuIanGor12
.

In this paper, we focus entirely on the labelled and nested proof-theoretic paradigms. The labelled paradigm may be qualified as
semantic
as calculi are built by transforming the semantic clauses and Kripke-frame properties of a logic into inference rules
Sim94
;
Vig00
. Despite some drawbacks and criticisms of this approach
Avr96
, the labelled paradigm offers many advantages. First, it is relatively straightforward to transform the semantics of a logic into a calculus; in fact, this process has been shown to be
automatable

CiaMafSpe13
. Second, the approach is exceptionally modular—allowing for the addition or deletion of rules to immediately obtain calculi for weaker or stronger logics—and is applicable to a wide variety of logics
DycNeg12
;
LyoBer19
;
Sim94
;
Vig00
. Last, labelled calculi consistently possess fundamental proof-theoretic properties such as invertibility of rules, admissibility of structural rules, and cut-admissibility—with fairly general results provided for large classes of modal, intuitionistic, and related logics
DycNeg12
;
LyoBer19
;
Sim94
;
Vig00
.
Although these characteristics are certainly favorable, a drawback of labelled calculi is that they typically involve a complicated syntax (which incorporates a large amount of semantic information), the sequents utilized in proofs encode general graphs, and inference rules often violate the subformula property (i.e. labelled calculi are not usually analytic). Such properties cause an unnecessary increase in the size of sequents/proofs, and a decrease in the efficiency of associated automated reasoning algorithms.

In contrast to the data structures (called,
labelled sequents
) employed in labelled calculi—which can be viewed as general graphs—the nested paradigm employs treelike data structures (called,
nested sequents
) which manipulate logical information and are used to derive theorems. The inception of the paradigm is often attributed to Bull
Bul92
and Kashima
Kas94
, though it should be noted that nested calculi can be considered ‘upside down’ versions of prefixed tableaux calculi, which were introduced much earlier in 1972 by Fitting
Fit72
. (NB. See
Fit14
for a discussion on the relationship between nested and tableaux systems). A strength of the nested paradigm is that the nested sequents employed reduce the bureaucracy and syntactic structures appearing in proofs, showing the nested formalism to be more parsimonious than the labelled formalism. Also, the nested formalism has proven itself useful in applications such as constructing analytic calculi
Bru09
;
Pog09Trends
, developing automated reasoning methods
TiuIanGor12
, and verifying interpolation
LyoTiuGorClo20
. Still, in spite of these advantages, the construction of nested calculi and the confirmation of their proof-theoretic properties is often done on a case-by-case basis. That is to say, the nested paradigm lacks general results—like those of the labelled paradigm—regarding the immediate construction of calculi in possession of fundamental properties.

Due to the fact that the labelled formalism is well-suited for constructing calculi possessing essential proof-theoretic properties, and the nested formalism is more refined and better suited for a variety of applications, a method of extracting nested calculi from labelled calculi—with the properties of the latter preserved—is highly desirable. This
refinement
process allows us to capture the best of both worlds: we invoke the general results of the labelled setting to obtain satisfactory labelled calculi for a class of logics, and via refinement, transform the systems into nested calculi better suited for applications. Similar ideas and relationships have been discussed in the literature
GorRam12AIML
;
LyoBer19
;
Lyo20
;
Mina13
;
Pim18
, where refined calculi (which can be considered nested calculi) were derived from labelled calculi for modal, intuitionistic, and related logics. (NB. The paper
Pim18
mentions results strongly related to Sect.
5
. Although the results presented here were discovered independently,
the work of Sect.
5
can be seen as a detailed explication and expansion of the work presented in
Pim18
. Moreover,
Pim18
does not consider the non-trivial and interesting first-order cases considered here.)

In this paper we advance our understanding of the aforementioned method, and show how to extract
slight
variants of Fitting’s nested calculi for propositional intuitionistic logic, first-order intuitionistic logic with non-constant domains, and first-order intuitionistic logic with constant domains from the labelled calculi for these logics. Additionally, we demonstrate the converse translation—showing how to transform each considered nested calculus into its associated labelled calculus. These translations are worthwhile in that they show how each nested calculus inherits properties from its corresponding labelled calculus, and also shed light on how the semantics of each logic affects the shape of rules and syntactic structures inherent in nested derivations (via the labelled calculi).

The organization of this paper is as follows: Sect.
2
introduces the semantics and axiomatizations for the intuitionistic logics we will consider. Sect.
3
introduces the labelled and nested calculi for these logics. Sect.
4
introduces preliminary definitions and lemmata sufficient to translate intuitionistic labelled calculi into nested calculi, and vice-versa. Sect.
5
, Sect.
6
, and Sect.
7
show how to refine each labelled calculus through structural rule elimination, allowing for the extraction of the nested calculus from the labelled calculus for propositional intuitionistic logic, first-order intuitionistic logic with non-constant domains, and first-order intuitionisitic logic with constant domains, respectively. Sect.
8
shows how to translate each nested calculus into its associated labelled calculus, and discusses corollaries of the translational correspondence between the calculi—primarily focusing on the properties inherited by each nested calculus from its corresponding labelled calculus. The last section, Sect.
9
, concludes.

This paper serves as an enhanced and revised version of the conference paper
Lyo20
. Most significantly, the nested-to-labelled translation of Sect.
4
, the content of Sect.
6
, and the majority of content in Sect.
8
are entirely new. Beyond this, the paper was written with an increased focus and more detailed exposition on
how
the labelled calculi are refined in order to extract each nested calculus—this provides the paper with more explanatory force than
Lyo20
. Also, it should be noted that this paper corrects an error that occurs in the conference version. In
Lyo20
, the labelled calculus
\mathsf{G3IntQC}
is lacking a structural rule (called
(ihd)
in this paper) corresponding to the condition that domains in first-order intuitionistic models are
non-empty
, or
inhabited
. Without the inclusion of this rule,
\mathsf{G3IntQC}
is incomplete as modus ponens cannot be simulated in the calculus (see Thm.
3.1
and Appendix
A
for details). We have included this rule here and adjusted the content of
Lyo20
regarding
\mathsf{G3IntQC}
accordingly. Furthermore, to increase the flow and readability of the paper, some results outside the scope of, or auxiliary to, our main focus (i.e. the translational correspondence between labelled and nested calculi for intuitionistic logics) have been moved to a technical appendix (Appendix
A
) for the interested reader.

2
Logical Preliminaries

In this section, we introduce the language, semantics, and axiomatizations for propositional intuitionistic logic
\mathsf{Int}
, first-order intuitionistic logic with non-constant domains
\mathsf{IntQ}
, and first-order intuitionistic logic with constant domains
\mathsf{IntQC}
. The first subsection will discuss the propositional setting, whereas the second subsection will discuss the first-order setting.

2.1
Propositional Intuitionistic Logic

The propositional language
\mathcal{L}
is defined via the BNF grammar shown below:

A::=p\ |\ \bot\ |\ (A\vee A)\ |\ (A\wedge A)\ |\ (A\supset A)

where
p
is among a denumerable set of
propositional variables

\mathrm{Prop}=\{p,q,r,\ldots\}
. As usual, we define intuitionistic negation as
\neg A:=A\supset\bot
. Moreover, the language admits a relational (or, Kripke-style) semantics as defined below (cf.
Kri65
).

Definition 1
(
\mathsf{Int}
-Frame,
\mathsf{Int}
-Model)

An
\mathsf{Int}
-frame
is an ordered pair
F=(W,\leq)
such that:

\blacktriangleright

W
is a non-empty set of worlds
\{w,u,v,\ldots\}
;

\blacktriangleright

\leq\ \subseteq W\times W
is a reflexive and transitive binary relation on
W
.
1
1

1

The properties imposed on
\leq
are defined as follows: (reflexivity) for all
w\in W
,
w\leq w
, and (transitivity) for all
w,u,v\in W
, if
w\leq v
and
v\leq u
, then
w\leq u
.

An
\mathsf{Int}
-model
is an ordered pair
M=(F,V)
where
F
is an
\mathsf{Int}
-frame and
V:\mathrm{Prop}\mapsto 2^{W}
is a
valuation function
mapping propositional variables to subsets of
W
satisfying the following
monotonicity condition
:

\mathbf{(M)}
If
w\in V(p)
and
w\leq v
, then
v\in V(p)
.

Definition 2
(Propositional Semantic Clauses)

Let
M=(W,\leq,V)
be an
\mathsf{Int}
-model with
w\in W
. The
satisfaction relation

M,w\Vdash A
between
w\in W
and a formula
A
from
\mathcal{L}
is inductively defined as follows:

\blacktriangleright

M,w\not\Vdash\bot
;

\blacktriangleright

M,w\Vdash p
iff
w\in V(p)
;

\blacktriangleright

M,w\Vdash A\vee B
iff
M,w\Vdash A
or
M,w\Vdash B
;

\blacktriangleright

M,w\Vdash A\land B
iff
M,w\Vdash A
and
M,w\Vdash B
;

\blacktriangleright

M,w\Vdash A\supset B
iff for all
u\in W
, if
w\leq u
and
M,u\Vdash A
, then
M,u\Vdash B
.

We say that a formula
A
is
globally true on
M
, written
M\Vdash A
, iff
M,u\Vdash A
for all worlds
u\in W
. A formula
A
is
\mathsf{Int}
-valid
, written
\Vdash_{\mathsf{Int}}A
, iff it is globally true on all
\mathsf{Int}
-models. Last, we say that a set
\Phi
of formulae
semantically implies
a formula
A
, written
\Phi\Vdash A
, iff for all intuitionistic models
M
with
w\in W
, if
M,w\Vdash B
for all
B\in\Phi
, then
M,w\Vdash A
.
2
2

2

We note that we could define a
global
version of semantic implication as follows: A set of formulae
\Phi

globally implies
a formula
A
iff for all intuitionistic models
M
, if
M\Vdash B
for all
B\in\Phi
, then
M\Vdash A
. We make use of the local version in Def.
2
however, because the axiomatization we use for
\mathsf{Int}
(shown in Fig.
2
) is sound and complete relative to the local version of semantic implication (Thm.
2.1
)
GabSheSkv09
.

The monotonicity condition
\mathbf{(M)}
, together with the intuitionistic semantics defined above, necessitates a general form of monotonicity as detailed below:

Lemma 1
(General Monotonicity)

Let
M
be a model with
w,v\in W
of
M
. If
M,w\Vdash A
and
w\leq v
, then
M,v\Vdash A
.

Proof

See
(
GabSheSkv09
, Lem. 3.2.16)
for details.
∎

\mathsf{Int}
is finitely axiomatizable. The axioms and inference rule syntactically characterizing
\mathsf{Int}
are given in Fig.

-derivation
(relative to the axiomatization of

is equivalent to the syntactic notion of an

-derivation from a set of formulae:

(Soundness and Completeness
GabSheSkv09
)

For any
A\in\mathcal{L}
,
\Phi\Vdash A
iff
\Phi\vdash A
.

2.2
First-Order Intuitionistic Logics

The language
\mathcal{Q}
for our first-order logics is defined via the BNF grammar below:

A::=p(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\ |\ \bot\ |\ (A\vee A)\ |\ (A\land A)\ |\ (A\supset A)\ |\ (\forall x)A\ |\ (\exists x)A

where
p
is among a denumerable set of
n
-ary
predicate symbols

\mathrm{Pred}=\{p,q,r,\ldots\}
and
x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},x
are
variables
(with
n\in\mathbb{N}
). We refer to formulae of the form
p(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})
as
atomic formulae
when
n>0
, and refer to formulae of the form
p
as
propositional variables
when
n=0
(i.e. a
0
-ary predicate
p
is a propositional variable). Furthermore, we define a variable
x
to be a
free variable
in
A
iff it is not within the scope of a quantifier
\forall x
or
\exists x
, and to be a
bound variable
iff it is within the scope of a quantifier. Last, as in the propositional case, our language admits a relational semantics, defined below.

Definition 3
(
\mathsf{IntQ}
-Frames,
\mathsf{IntQ}
-Models
GabSheSkv09
)

We define an
\mathsf{IntQ}
-frame
to be a tuple
F=(W,\leq,D)
such that:

\blacktriangleright

W
is a non-empty set of worlds
\{w,u,v,\ldots\}
;

\blacktriangleright

\leq\ \subseteq W\times W
is a reflexive and transitive binary relation on
W
;

\blacktriangleright

D
is a
domain function
mapping a world
w\in W
to a non-empty set
D_{w}
of
objects

\{a,b,c,\dots\}
satisfying the
nested domain condition
shown below:

\mathbf{(ND)}
If
a\in D_{w}
and
w\leq v
, then
a\in D_{v}
.

A
\mathsf{IntQC}
-frame
is an
\mathsf{IntQ}
-frame
that additionally satisfies the following
constant domain condition
shown below:

\mathbf{(CD)}
If
a\in D_{v}
and
w\leq v
, then
a\in D_{w}
.

An
\mathsf{IntQ}
-model
(
\mathsf{IntQC}
-model
)
M
is an ordered pair
(F,V)
where
F
is an
\mathsf{IntQ}
-frame (
\mathsf{IntQC}
-frame) and
V
is a
valuation function
such that
V(p,w)\subseteq(D_{w})^{n}
(with
n\in\mathbb{N}
) satisfying the following
monotonicity condition
:

\mathbf{(M)}
If
w\in V(p,w)
and
w\leq v
, then
v\in V(p,v)
(if
p
is of arity
0
);

If
w\leq v
, then
V(p,w)\subseteq V(p,v)
(if
p
is of arity
n>0
).

We uphold the convention in
GabSheSkv09
and assume that for each world
w\in W
,
(D_{w})^{0}=\{w\}
, so
V(p,w)=\{w\}
or
V(p,w)=\emptyset
, for a propositional variable
p
.

As in
GabSheSkv09
, we forgo the direct interpretation of formulae from
\mathcal{Q}
on relational models, and instead, introduce
D_{w}
-sentences (Def.
4
) to be interpreted on such models. Defining satisfaction relative to
D_{w}
-sentences gives rise to a notion of validity for formulae in
\mathcal{Q}
(Def.
5
). However, this notion of validity also depends on the
universal closure
of a formula: given that
A\in\mathcal{Q}
contains only
x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}
as free variables, the universal closure

Definition 4
(
D_{w}
-Sentence)

Let
M=(W,\leq,D,V)
be an
\mathsf{IntQ}
-model with
w\in W
. We define
\mathcal{Q}({D_{w}})
to be the language
\mathcal{Q}
expanded with parameters
\underline{a},\underline{b},\underline{c},\ldots
corresponding to the objects in the set
D_{w}=\{a,b,c,\ldots\}
. We define a
D_{w}
-formula
to be a formula in
\mathcal{Q}(D_{w})
, and we define a
D_{w}
-sentence
to be a
D_{w}
-formula that does not contain any free variables.

Definition 5
(First-Order Semantic Clauses)

Let
M=(W,\leq,D,V)
be an
\mathsf{IntQ}
- or
\mathsf{IntQC}
-model with
w\in W
. The
satisfaction relation

M,w\Vdash A
between
w
and a
D_{w}
-sentence
A
is inductively defined as follows:

\blacktriangleright

If
p
is a propositional variable, then
M,w\Vdash p
iff
w\in V(p,w)
;

\blacktriangleright

If
p
is an
n
-ary predicate symbol
(
with
n>0)
, then
M,w\Vdash p(\underline{a}_{1},\cdots,\underline{a}_{n})
iff
(a_{1},\cdots,a_{n})\in V(p,w)
;

\blacktriangleright

M,w\Vdash\forall xA
iff for all
v\in W
and all
a\in D_{v}
, if
w\leq v
, then
M,v\Vdash A(\underline{a}/x)
;

\blacktriangleright

M,w\Vdash\exists xA
iff there exists an
a\in D_{w}
such that
M,w\Vdash A(\underline{a}/x)
.

The clauses for the
\lor
,
\land
, and
\supset
connectives are the same as in Def.
2
.
We say that a formula
A
is
globally true on
M
, written
M\Vdash A
, iff
M,u\Vdash\forall\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\mkern for all worlds

. A formula
A
is
\mathsf{IntQ}
-valid
(
\mathsf{IntQC}
-valid
), written
\Vdash_{\mathsf{IntQ}}A
(
\Vdash_{\mathsf{IntQC}}A
, resp.), iff it is globally true on all
\mathsf{IntQ}
-models (
\mathsf{IntQC}
-models).

Similar to the propositional case, the monotonicity condition imposed on atomic formulae in models generalizes:

Lemma 2
(General Monotonicity)

Let
M
be an
\mathsf{IntQ}
- or
\mathsf{IntQC}
-model with
w,v\in W
of
M
. For any
D_{w}
-sentence
A
, if
M,w\Vdash A
and
w\leq v
, then
M,v\Vdash A
.

Proof

See
(
GabSheSkv09
, Lem. 3.2.16)
for details.
∎

Sound and complete axiomatizations for our first-order intuitionistic logics (viz.
\mathsf{IntQ}
and
\mathsf{IntQC}
) are provided in Fig.
3
. We define the
substitution

(y/x)
of the variable
y
for the free variable
x
on a formula
A
in the standard way as the replacement of all free occurrences of
x
in
A
with
y
. Last, the side condition
y
is free for
x
(see Fig.
3
) is taken to mean that
y
does not become bound by a quantifier if substituted for
x
.

\forall x(B\supset A)\supset(B\supset\forall xA)~\textit{ with $x\not\in B$}\qquad\forall x(A\supset B)\supset(\exists xA\supset B)~\textit{ with $x\not\in B$}

\forall xA\supset A(y/x)~\textit{y free for x}\qquad A(y/x)\supset\exists xA~\textit{y free for x}\qquad\forall xAA

\forall x(A\vee B)\supset\forall xA\vee B~\textit{ with $x\not\in B$}

Figure 3:
The axiomatization for the logic
\mathsf{IntQ}
is given by extending the axiomatization of
\mathsf{Int}
with the first two rows. The axiomatization for the logic
\mathsf{IntQC}
is given by extending the axiomatization of
\mathsf{Int}
with all three rows. Both axiomatizations can be found in
GabSheSkv09
.

The logics
\mathsf{IntQ}
and
\mathsf{IntQC}
are defined to be the smallest set of formulae from
\mathcal{Q}
closed under substitutions of the axioms and applications of the inference rules in their axiomatizations. The sole difference between the axiomatizations for
\mathsf{IntQ}
and
\mathsf{IntQC}
is that the former omits the
constant domain axiom

\forall x(A\vee B)\supset\forall xA\vee B
(with
x\not\in B
) whereas the latter includes it. We write
\vdash_{\mathsf{IntQ}}A
(
\vdash_{\mathsf{IntQC}}A
) to denote that
A
is an element, or
theorem
, of
\mathsf{IntQ}
(
\mathsf{IntQC}
, resp.).

Theorem 2.2
(Soundness and Completeness
GabSheSkv09
)

For any
A\in\mathcal{Q}
,
\Vdash_{\mathsf{IntQ}}A
(
\Vdash_{\mathsf{IntQC}}A
) iff
\vdash_{\mathsf{IntQ}}A
(
\vdash_{\mathsf{IntQC}}A
, resp.).

3
Proof Calculi for Intuitionistic Logics

In this section, we introduce the labelled and nested proof systems for the intuitionistic logics
\mathsf{Int}
,
\mathsf{IntQ}
, and
\mathsf{IntQC}
. The first subsection presents the labelled system
\mathsf{G3Int}
for propositional intuitionistic logic from
DycNeg12
as well as the first-order extensions of this calculus, that makes use of quantifier and structural rules motivated by those (viz.
\forall L
,
\forall R
,
id
, and
dd
) given in
(
Vig00
, Ch. 6)
. The second subsection introduces (slight variants of) Fitting’s nested calculi for intuitionistic logics from
Fit14
.

3.1
The Labelled Calculi
\mathsf{G3Int}
,
\mathsf{G3IntQ}
, and
\mathsf{G3IntQC}

We define
propositional
(
first-order
)
labelled sequents
to be syntactic objects of the form
L_{1}\Rightarrow L_{2}
(
L_{1}^{\prime}\Rightarrow L_{2}^{\prime}
, resp.), where
L_{1}
and
L_{2}
(
L_{1}^{\prime}
and
L_{2}^{\prime}
, resp.) are formulae defined via the BNF grammar below top (below bottom, resp.).

L_{1}::=\varepsilon\ |\ w:A\ |\ w\leq v\ |\ L_{1},L_{1}

L_{2}::=\varepsilon\ |\ w:A\ |\ L_{2},L_{2}

L_{1}^{\prime}::=\varepsilon\ |\ w:A\ |\ \underline{a}\in D_{w}\ |\ w\leq v\ |\ L_{1}^{\prime},L_{1}^{\prime}

L_{2}^{\prime}::=\varepsilon\ |\ w:A\ |\ L_{2}^{\prime},L_{2}^{\prime}

In the propositional case,
A
is in the language
\mathcal{L}
and
w
is among a denumerable set of labels
\{w,v,u,\ldots\}
. In the first-order case,
A
is in the language
\mathcal{Q}
,
\underline{a}
is among a denumerable set of
parameters

\{\underline{a},\underline{b},\underline{c},\ldots\}
, and
w
is among a denumerable set of labels
\{w,v,u,\ldots\}
. We refer to formulae of the forms
w\leq v
and
\underline{a}\in D_{w}
as
relational atoms
(with formulae of the form
\underline{a}\in D_{w}
sometimes referred to as
domain atoms
, more specifically) and refer to formulae of the form
w:A
as
labelled formulae
. Due to the two types of formulae occurring in a labelled sequent, we often use
\mathcal{R}
to denote relational atoms, and
\Gamma
and
\Delta
to denote labelled formulae, thus distinguishing between the two. Labelled sequents are therefore written in a general form as
\mathcal{R},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta
.

\mathcal{R},w\leq v,w:p,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,v:p

(see

). The labelled calculus
\mathsf{G3IntQ}
for
\mathsf{IntQ}
consists of all rules minus the

rule, and all rules give the calculus
\mathsf{G3IntQC}
for
\mathsf{IntQC}
. The side condition
{\dagger}_{1}
states that the variable
v
does not occur in the conclusion,
{\dagger}_{2}
states that
\underline{a}
does not occur in the conclusion, and
{\dagger}_{3}
states that neither
\underline{a}
nor
v
occurs in the conclusion. Labels and parameters restricted from occurring in the conclusion of an inference are called
eigenvariables
.

Moreover, we take the comma operator to be commutative and associative; for example, we identify the labelled sequent
w\leq u,w:A,\underline{a}\in D_{w}\Rightarrow v:C,u:B
with
\underline{a}\in D_{w},w\leq u,w:A\Rightarrow u:B,v:C
. This interpretation of comma lets us view
\mathcal{R},\Gamma
(the
antecedent
) and
\Delta
(the
succedent
) of a labelled sequent
\mathcal{R},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta
as multisets. Also, we use
\varepsilon
to denote the
empty string
which acts as the identity element for the comma operator (e.g. we identify
w\leq v,\varepsilon,v:B
with
w\leq v,v:B
), and we stipulate that if
\varepsilon
is the antecedent or succedent of a sequent, then the antecedent or succedent is left empty. Therefore,
\varepsilon
will be implicit in labelled sequents, but will never explicitly appear.

In the first-order setting, we syntactically distinguish between
bound variables

\{x,y,z,\ldots\}
and
free variables
, which are replaced with
parameters

\{\underline{a},\underline{b},\underline{c},\ldots\}
, to avoid clashes between the two categories (cf.
(
Fit14
, Sect. 8)
). Therefore, instead of using formulae directly from the first-order language, we use formulae from the first-order language where each freely occurring variable
x
has been replaced by a distinct parameter
\underline{a}
. For example, we would make use of the labelled formula
w:(\forall x)p(\underline{a},x)\lor q(\underline{a},\underline{b})
instead of
w:(\forall x)p(y,x)\lor q(y,z)
in a first-order sequent. Last, we use the notation
A(\underline{a}_{1},\ldots,\underline{a}_{n})
, with
n\in\mathbb{N}
, to denote that the parameters
\underline{a}_{1},\ldots,\underline{a}_{n}
are all parameters occurring in the formula
A
. (NB. We will occasionally abuse notation and write
A(\underline{a})
to indicate that the formula
A
contains a parameter
\underline{a}
in which we are interested; however, when using this notation we leave open the possibility that
A
may contain other parameters as well.) We write

as shorthand for
\underline{a}_{1}\in D_{w},\ldots,\underline{a}_{n}\in D_{w}
. The labelled calculi are given in Fig.
4
.

Each labelled calculus is obtained from the models and semantic clauses of
\mathsf{Int}
,
\mathsf{IntQ}
, and
\mathsf{IntQC}
. We note that the labelled calculus
\mathsf{G3Int}
for
\mathsf{Int}
is presented in
DycNeg12
, whereas the labelled calculi
\mathsf{G3IntQ}
and
\mathsf{G3IntQC}
for
\mathsf{IntQ}
and
\mathsf{IntQC}
(respectively) are new. The rules
(\bot_{l})
,
(\wedge_{l})
,
(\wedge_{r})
,
(\vee_{l})
,
(\vee_{r})
,
(\supset_{l})
,
(\supset_{r})
,
(\exists_{l})
,
(\exists_{r})
,
(\forall_{l})
, and
(\forall_{r})
are rule representations of the semantic clauses given in Def.
2
and Def.
5
. The
(ref)
and
(tra)
rules allow inferences arising from the fact that frames are reflexive and transitive, whereas
(ihd)
,
(nd)
, and
(cd)
allow inferences based on the fact that the domains of frames are always inhabited (i.e. non-empty), are nested, and are constant, respectively. The rules
(id)
and
(id_{q})
encode the monotonicity condition imposed on models; note that
(id)
is an instance of
(id_{q})
(the same holds for the corresponding rules in the nested setting, which are introduced in the next subsection). Last, we write
\vdash_{\mathsf{G3Int}}\Lambda
,
\vdash_{\mathsf{G3IntQ}}\Lambda
, and
\vdash_{\mathsf{G3IntQC}}\Lambda
to indicate that the labelled sequent
\Lambda
is derivable in
\mathsf{G3Int}
,
\mathsf{G3IntQ}
, and
\mathsf{G3IntQC}
, respectively—this notation extends straightforwardly to the other calculi we will consider.

We define a
label substitution

(w/v)
on a multiset of labelled formulae or relational atoms in the usual way as the replacement of all labels
v
occurring in the mulitset with the label
w
. Similarly, we define a
parameter substitution

(\underline{a}/\underline{b})
on a multiset of labelled formulae or relational atoms as the replacement of all parameters
\underline{b}
occurring in the multiset with the parameter
\underline{a}
.

Our labelled calculi possess desirable proof-theoretic properties such as the
height-preserving (hp-) admissibility
of substitutions and structural rules (e.g.
(psub)
and
(wk)
), the
height-preserving (hp-) invertibility
of all rules, and admissibility of
(cut)
. These properties are detailed in the theorem below (Thm.
3.1
) with the (hp-)admissible rules shown in Fig.
5
.

\mathcal{R}(w/v),\Gamma(w/v)\Rightarrow\Delta(w/v)

\mathcal{R},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

(psub)

\mathcal{R}(\underline{a}/\underline{b}),\Gamma(\underline{a}/\underline{b})\Rightarrow\Delta(\underline{a}/\underline{b})

\mathcal{R},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

(wk)

\mathcal{R}^{\prime},\mathcal{R},\Gamma^{\prime},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta^{\prime},\Delta

\mathcal{R},\mathcal{R}^{\prime},\mathcal{R}^{\prime},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

\mathcal{R},\mathcal{R}^{\prime},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

(ctr_{r})

3.2
The Nested Calculi
\mathsf{NInt}
,
\mathsf{NIntQ}
, and
\mathsf{NIntQC}

We define a propositional (or, first-order) nested sequent
\Sigma
to be a syntactic object defined via the following BNF grammars:

X::=\varepsilon\ |\ A\ |\ X,X

\Sigma::=X\rightarrow X\ |\ X\rightarrow X,[\Sigma],\ldots,[\Sigma]

where
A
is in the propositional language
\mathcal{L}
(first-order language
\mathcal{Q}
, resp.). As in the previous section, we take the comma operator to be commutative and associative, allowing us to view syntactic entities
X
as multisets, and we let
\varepsilon
represent the empty string which—as in the labelled setting—occurs implicitly, but not explicitly, in sequents.

In the first-order setting, we syntactically distinguish between bound variables and free variables in first-order formulae, using
\{x,y,z,\ldots\}
for bound variables and replacing the occurrence of free variables in formulae with parameters
\{\underline{a},\underline{b},\underline{c},\ldots\}
. For example, we would use
p(\underline{a})\rightarrow p(\underline{b}),[\bot\rightarrow\forall xq(x,\underline{b})]
instead of the sequent
p(x)\rightarrow p(y),[\bot\rightarrow\forall xq(x,y)]
in a nested derivation (where the free variable
x
has been replaced by the parameter
\underline{a}
and
y
has been replaced by
\underline{b}
).

Nested sequents are often written as
\Sigma\{X\rightarrow Y,[\Sigma_{1}],\ldots,[\Sigma_{n}]\}
, which indicates that
X\rightarrow Y,[\Sigma_{1}],\ldots,[\Sigma_{n}]
occurs at some depth in the nestings of the sequent
\Sigma
. For example, if
\Sigma
is taken to be
p(\underline{a})\rightarrow[\bot\rightarrow\forall xq(x,\underline{b}),[\ \rightarrow\top]]
, then
\Sigma\{\bot\rightarrow\forall xq(x,\underline{b})\}
,
\Sigma\{\bot\rightarrow\forall xq(x,\underline{b}),[\ \rightarrow\top]\}
, and
\Sigma\{\rightarrow\top\}
are correct representations of
\Sigma
in our notation.

The nested calculi are given in Fig.
6
and are
slight
variants of the calculi presented by Fitting in
Fit14
. The only difference is that the rules
(\neg_{l})
,
(lift)
,
(\supset_{l})
,
(\exists_{r})
, and
(\forall_{l})
preserve copies of the principal formula in the premise of the rule. Since we will be extracting Fitting’s nested calculi from our labelled calculi, it will be seen that these copies of principal formulae are residua of this process, which is based on the fact that our labelled calculi preserve copies of principal formulae in the premise(s) of certain rules. Howbeit, it is easy to confirm that the calculi
\mathsf{NInt}
,
\mathsf{NIntQ}
, and
\mathsf{NIntQC}
are equivalent to Fitting’s calculi from
Fit14

The two distinguishing factors between the nested calculi

(\forall^{c}_{r})

, which we define below:

Definition 6
(Available Parameter
Fit14
)

Let
\Sigma\{X\rightarrow Y,[\Sigma_{1}],\ldots,[\Sigma_{n}]\}
be a nested sequent. If there exists a formula
A(\underline{a})\in X,Y
, then the parameter
\underline{a}
is available in
X\rightarrow Y
and in all boxed subsequents
\Sigma_{i}
(with
i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}
).

As explained in the following section, a nested sequent can be seen as a tree of sequents of the form
X\rightarrow Y
. Intuitively, if a parameter is available at some point
X\rightarrow Y
in the tree, then it will be available at all points in the future of that point, i.e. in the subtree with
X\rightarrow Y
as its root. Since a nested sequent can be seen as an abstraction of an
\mathsf{IntQ}
-model encoding the model’s underlying treelike structure, the notion of an available parameter corresponds to the fact that if a parameter denotes an object in the domain of a world, then—due to the nested domain condition (Def.
3
)—that parameter denotes that object at all future worlds and is
available
for use in sentences at such worlds.

A feature which distinguishes the nested formalism from the labelled is that nested sequents may readily be converted into an
equivalent formula
, that is, nested sequents allow for a straightforward formula translation (see Def.
7
below). As a consequence of our refinement procedure, we will see in Sect.
8
(viz. Cor.
4
) that a nested sequent
\Sigma
is provable if and only if its formula interpretation is provable.

Definition 7
(Formula Interpretation)

The

\iota(X\rightarrow Y):=\displaystyle{\bigwedge X\supset\bigvee Y}

\iota(X\rightarrow Y,[\Sigma_{1}],\ldots,[\Sigma_{n}]):=\displaystyle{\bigwedge X\supset\bigg(\bigvee Y\vee\bigvee_{1\leq i\leq n}\iota(\Sigma_{i})\bigg)}

In the propositional setting,
\iota(\Sigma)
is a formula in
\mathcal{L}

\Sigma
as a formula in
\mathcal{Q}

Proof-theoretic properties of

\mathsf{IntQ}

Theorem 3.2
(Soundness and Completeness)

\mathsf{NInt}
,
\mathsf{NIntQ}
, and
\mathsf{NIntQC}
are strongly sound and complete for
\mathsf{Int}
,
\mathsf{IntQ}
, and
\mathsf{IntQC}
, respectively.

Interestingly, the correspondence we establish between
\mathsf{G3Int}
and
\mathsf{NInt}
, and
\mathsf{G3IntQC}
and
\mathsf{NIntQC}
, can be leveraged to show that
\mathsf{NInt}
and

inherit soundness and completeness from their associated labelled calculi. The correspondence between
\mathsf{NIntQ}
and

cannot be leveraged to conclude the completeness of
\mathsf{NIntQ}
however, because of the use of a lemma (Lem.
14
in Sect.
6
) that invokes the strong completeness of
\mathsf{NIntQ}
(i.e. it invokes Thm.
3.2
above). Still, we note in that section how the lemma may be proved independent of the completeness of
\mathsf{NIntQ}
, thus allowing for
\mathsf{NIntQ}
to inherit the completeness of
\mathsf{G3IntQ}
via our refinement and translation processes. Last, in Sect.

, we will show that our nested calculi inherit additional properties from their corresponding labelled calculi such as the admissibilty of certain structural rules (Cor.
2
) and the invertibility of all rules (Cor.
3
).

4
Fundamentals for Establishing Correspondence

This section consists of two parts: in the first subsection, we define translation functions that transform labelled sequents into nested sequents and vice-versa, as well as define classes of labelled sequents that are fruitful for carrying out our proof-theoretic transformation and translation work. In the second subsection, we establish preliminary results that are convenient for refining our labelled calculi, that is, such results will assist us in eliminating the structural rules (e.g.
(ref)
and
(nd)
) from
\mathsf{G3Int}
,
\mathsf{G3IntQ}
, and
\mathsf{G3IntQC}
(which will ultimately yield systems that are close variants of Fitting’s nested systems).

4.1
Translating Notation: Labelled and Nested

It is instructive to observe that both nested and labelled sequents can be viewed as graphs (with the former restricted to trees and the latter more general). Graphs of sequents are significant for two reasons: the first (technical) reason is that graphs can be leveraged to switch from labelled to nested notation; thus, graphs will play a role in deriving our nested calculi from our labelled calculi, and vice-versa. Second, graphs offer insight into
why
structural rule elimination yields nested systems, which will be discussed in the next section (Sect.
5
).

It is straightforward to define the graph of each type of sequent. To do this, we first introduce a bit of notation and define the multiset
\Gamma\restriction w:=\{A\ |\ w:A\in\Gamma\}
. For a labelled sequent
\Lambda:=\mathcal{R},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta
, the
graph

G(\Lambda)
is the tuple
(V,E,\lambda)
, where (i)
V:=\{w\ |\ \text{$w$ is a label in $\Lambda$.}\}
, (ii)
(w,v)\in E
iff
w\leq v\in\mathcal{R}
, and

(iii)\quad\lambda:=\{(w,\Gamma^{\prime}\Rightarrow\Delta^{\prime})\ |\ \Gamma^{\prime}=\Gamma\restriction w\text{, }\Delta^{\prime}=\Delta\restriction w\text{, and }w\in V\}.

For a nested sequent, the graph is defined inductively on the structure of the nestings; we use strings
\sigma
of natural numbers to denote vertices in the graph, similar to the prefixes used in prefixed tableaux
Fit72
;
Fit12
;
Fit14
.

Base case.
Let our nested sequent be of the form
X\rightarrow Y
with
X
and
Y
multisets of formulae. Then,
G_{\sigma}(X\rightarrow Y):=(V_{\sigma},E_{\sigma},\lambda_{\sigma})
, where (i)
V_{\sigma}:=\{\sigma\}
, (ii)
E_{\sigma}:=\emptyset
, and (iii)
\lambda_{\sigma}:=\{(\sigma,X\rightarrow Y)\}
.

Inductive step.
Suppose our nested sequent is of the form
X\rightarrow Y,[\Sigma_{1}],\ldots,[\Sigma_{n}]
. We assume that each
G_{\sigma.i}(\Sigma_{i})=(V_{\sigma.i},E_{\sigma.i},\lambda_{\sigma.i})
(with
i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}
) is already defined, and define
G_{\sigma}(X\rightarrow Y,[\Sigma_{1}],\ldots,[\Sigma_{n}]):=(V_{\sigma},E_{\sigma},\lambda_{\sigma})
as follows:

(i)\quad V_{\sigma}:=\{\sigma\}\cup\displaystyle{\bigcup_{1\leq i\leq n}V_{\sigma.i}}\qquad(ii)\quad E_{\sigma}:=\{(\sigma,\sigma.i)\ |\ 1\leq i\leq n\}\cup\displaystyle{\bigcup_{1\leq i\leq n}E_{\sigma.i}}

(iii)\quad\lambda_{\sigma}:=\{(\sigma,X\rightarrow Y)\}\cup\displaystyle{\bigcup_{1\leq i\leq n}\lambda_{\sigma.i}}

We will occasionally refer to a sequent of the form
X\rightarrow Y
in a nested sequent
\Sigma
such that
(\sigma,X\rightarrow Y)\in\lambda_{0}
(with
G_{0}(\Sigma)=(V_{0},E_{0},\lambda_{0})
) as a
component
of the nested sequent
\Sigma
.

Definition 8

Let
G_{0}=(V_{0},E_{0},\lambda_{0})
and
G_{1}=(V_{1},E_{1},\lambda_{1})
be two graphs. We define an
isomorphism

f:V_{0}\mapsto V_{1}
between
G_{0}
and
G_{1}
to be a function such that: (i)
f
is bijective, (ii)
(x,y)\in E_{0}
iff
(fx,fy)\in E_{1}
, (iii)
\lambda_{0}(x)=\lambda_{1}(fx)
. We say
G_{0}
and
G_{1}
are
isomorphic
iff there exists an isomorphism between them.

Although the formal definitions above may appear somewhat cumbersome, the example below shows that transforming a sequent into its graph—or conversely, obtaining the sequent from its graph—is relatively straightforward.

Example 1

The nested sequent
\Sigma
is given below with its corresponding graph
G_{0}(\Sigma)
shown on the left, and the labelled sequent
\Lambda
is given below with its corresponding graph
G(\Lambda)
on the right. Regarding the labelled sequent, we assume that
\Gamma_{i}
and

(for

).

\Sigma=X_{0}\rightarrow Y_{0},[X_{1}\rightarrow Y_{1},[X_{2}\rightarrow Y_{2}]],[X_{3}\rightarrow Y_{3}]

\textstyle{\underset{0}{\boxed{X_{0}\rightarrow Y_{0}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

\textstyle{\underset{w_{0}}{\boxed{\Gamma_{0}\restriction w_{0}\Rightarrow\Delta_{0}\restriction w_{0}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

\Lambda=w_{0}\leq w_{0},w_{0}\leq w_{1},w_{1}\leq w_{2},w_{0}\leq w_{2},w_{0}\leq w_{3},\Gamma_{0},\Gamma_{1},\Gamma_{2},\Gamma_{3}\Rightarrow\Delta_{0},\Delta_{1},\Delta_{2},\Delta_{3}

In the above example there is a loop from
w_{0}
to itself in the graph of the labelled sequent; furthermore, there is an undirected cycle occurring between
w_{0}
,
w_{1}
, and
w_{2}
. As will be explained in the next section (specifically, Thm.
5.2
), the
(ref)
and
(tra)
rules allow for such structures to appear in the graphs of labelled sequents used to derive theorems; however, the elimination of these rules in our labelled calculi has the effect that such structures
can no longer
occur in the labelled derivation of a theorem. Consequently, it will be seen that eliminating such rules yields a labelled derivation where every sequent has a purely
treelike
structure (cf.
GorRam12AIML
). This implies that each labelled sequent in the derivation has a graph isomorphic to the graph of a nested sequent. It is this idea which ultimately permits the extraction of our nested calculi from our labelled calculi.

Definition 9

Let
\Lambda
be a labelled sequent and
G(\Lambda)=(V,E,\lambda)
. We say that
\Lambda
is
treelike
iff there exists a unique vertex
w\in V
, called the
root
, such that there exists a unique path from
w
to every other vertex
v\in V
.
3
3

3

Treelike sequents are equivalently characterized as sequents with graphs that are: (i) connected, (ii) acyclic, and (iii) contain no backwards branching.
We say that a labelled derivation is
treelike
iff every labelled sequent in the derivation is treelike.

If we take the graph of a treelike labelled sequent, then it can be viewed as the graph of a nested sequent, as the example below demonstrates:

Example 2

The treelike labelled sequent
\Lambda^{\prime}
and its graph are given below. We assume that
\Gamma_{i}
and
\Delta_{i}
contain only formulae labelled with
w_{i}
(for
i\in\{0,1,2,3\}
).

\Lambda^{\prime}=w_{0}\leq w_{1},w_{1}\leq w_{2},w_{0}\leq w_{3},\Gamma_{0},\Gamma_{1},\Gamma_{2},\Gamma_{3}\Rightarrow\Delta_{0},\Delta_{1},\Delta_{2},\Delta_{3}

\textstyle{\underset{w_{2}}{\boxed{\Gamma_{2}^{\prime}\Rightarrow\Delta_{2}^{\prime}}}}
\textstyle{\underset{w_{1}}{\boxed{\Gamma_{1}^{\prime}\Rightarrow\Delta_{1}^{\prime}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\textstyle{\underset{w_{0}}{\boxed{\Gamma_{0}^{\prime}\Rightarrow\Delta_{0}^{\prime}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\textstyle{\underset{w_{3}}{\boxed{\Gamma_{3}^{\prime}\Rightarrow\Delta_{3}^{\prime}}}}

Also, if we assume that
\Gamma_{i}^{\prime}=\Gamma_{i}\restriction w_{i}=X_{i}
and
\Delta_{i}^{\prime}=\Delta_{i}\restriction w_{i}=Y_{i}
(for
i\in\{0,1,2,3\}
), then the above graph is isomorphic to the graph of the nested sequent in Example
1
, meaning that
\Lambda
can be translated as that nested sequent.

To make the above translation precise, we introduce the
w
-downward closure
of the graph of a labelled sequent. We may utilize this notion to explicitly define the
translation

\mathfrak{N}
(see Def.
11
) that translates labelled sequents into nested sequents. This translation will prove itself useful in extracting Fitting’s nested calculi from our labelled calculi.

Definition 10
(Downward Closure)

Let
\Lambda
be a treelike labelled sequent with graph
G(\Lambda)=(V,E,\lambda)
and
w\in V
. We define the
w
-downward closure

G_{w}(\Lambda)=(V^{\prime},E^{\prime},\lambda^{\prime})
to be the smallest subgraph of
G(\Lambda)
such that
w\in V^{\prime}
and

\blacktriangleright

if
v\in V^{\prime}
and
(v,u)\in E
, then
u\in V^{\prime}
;

\blacktriangleright

E^{\prime}=\{(u,v)\ |\ u,v\in V^{\prime}\}
;

\blacktriangleright

\lambda^{\prime}=\{(v,\Gamma^{\prime}\Rightarrow\Delta^{\prime})\ |\ v\in V^{\prime}\text{ and }(v,\Gamma^{\prime}\Rightarrow\Delta^{\prime})\in\lambda\}
.

Definition 11
(The Translation
\mathfrak{N}
)

Let
\Lambda
be a treelike labelled sequent with root
w
. We inductively define
\mathfrak{N}(\Lambda):=\mathfrak{N}(G_{w}(\Lambda))
to be the nested sequent obtained from the graph
G_{w}(\Lambda)
as follows:

\blacktriangleright

If
G_{u}(\Lambda)=(V,E,\lambda)
, where
V=\{u\}
,
E=\emptyset
, and
\lambda=\{(u,\Gamma^{\prime}\Rightarrow\Delta^{\prime})\}
, then

\mathfrak{N}(G_{u}(\Lambda)):=\Gamma^{\prime}\rightarrow\Delta^{\prime}.

\blacktriangleright

If
G_{u}(\Lambda)=(V,E,\lambda)
, where
u,v_{1},\ldots,v_{n}\in V
,
(u,v_{1}),\ldots,(u,v_{n})\in E
, and
(u,\Gamma^{\prime}\Rightarrow\Delta^{\prime})\in\lambda
, then

\mathfrak{N}(G_{u}(\Lambda)):=\Gamma^{\prime}\rightarrow\Delta^{\prime},[\mathfrak{N}(G_{v_{1}}(\Lambda))],\ldots,[\mathfrak{N}(G_{v_{n}}(\Lambda))].

We also define a converse translation
\mathfrak{L}
that translates nested sequents into labelled sequents. Whereas the former translation
\mathfrak{N}
is useful in extracting our nested calculi from our labelled calculi, the translation
\mathfrak{L}
is useful in transferring proof-theoretic properties of the latter to the former as well as establishing the converse translation (see Sect.
8
). In order to define this translation, we first define two operations: (i) If
X
is a multiset of formulae from
\mathcal{L}
or
\mathcal{Q}
, then
w:X:=\{w:A\ |\ A\in X\}
, that is,
w:X
is the multiset of all formulae from
X
labelled with
w
, and (ii) If
\Lambda_{1}=\mathcal{R}_{1},\Gamma_{1}\Rightarrow\Delta_{1}
and
\Lambda_{2}=\mathcal{R}_{2},\Gamma_{2}\Rightarrow\Delta_{2}
, then we define the
sequent composition

\Lambda_{1}\oplus\Lambda_{2}:=\mathcal{R}_{1},\mathcal{R}_{2},\Gamma_{1},\Gamma_{2}\Rightarrow\Delta_{1},\Delta_{2}
.

(The Translation
\mathfrak{L}
)

\Sigma
be a nested sequent. We inductively define
\mathfrak{L}(\Sigma):=\mathfrak{L}(G_{0}(\Sigma))
to be the labelled sequent obtained from the graph
G_{0}(\Sigma)
as follows:

\blacktriangleright

If
G_{\sigma}(\Sigma)=(V_{\sigma},E_{\sigma},\lambda_{\sigma})
with
V=\{\sigma\}
,
E=\emptyset
,
\lambda=\{(\sigma,X\rightarrow Y)\}
, and

\hfil\textstyle a\hfil

are all parameters occurring in
X,Y
, then

\oplus\Big(\mathfrak{L}(G_{\sigma.1}(\Sigma))\Big)\oplus\cdots\oplus\Big(\mathfrak{L}(G_{\sigma.n}(\Sigma))\Big)
.

To simplify notation when making use of the
\mathfrak{L}
translation, we will use the same labels
w
,
u
,
v
,
\ldots
employed in our labelled calculi in place of strings
\sigma
of natural numbers.

Before finishing this subsection, we introduce a fundamental notion useful for completing our translation from labelled to nested, which is based on the above definition—the notion of a
nestedlike
labelled sequent:

Definition 13
(Nestedlike)

We say that a labelled sequent
\Lambda
is
nestedlike
iff there exists a nested sequent
\Sigma
such that
\mathfrak{L}(\Sigma)=\Lambda
.

It is not difficult to see that the following lemma holds:

Lemma 3

Let
\Lambda:=\mathcal{R},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta
be a nestedlike labelled sequent. Then, (i)
\Lambda
is treelike, (ii)
\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{N}(\Lambda))=\Lambda
(up to a change in labels), and (iii) there exists a domain atom
\underline{a}\in D_{w}\in\mathcal{R}
iff there exists a labelled formula
w:A(\underline{a})\in\Gamma,\Delta
.

4.2
Setting the Stage for Refinement: Preliminary Results

In order to extract Fitting’s nested calculi from our labelled calculi, we will expand our labelled calculi with rules sufficient for the elimination of certain structural rules. Therefore, we first inflate our calculi to a large collection of rules, and use the new additions to systematically eliminate certain rules from each calculus, thus obtaining a refined variant of each calculus. To avoid lengthy names for our inflated and refined calculi, we will use the following abbreviations throughout the remainder of the paper (see Fig.
7
for newly introduced rules):

\mathsf{G3IntQ}^{*}

,
\mathsf{G3IntQ}
, and
\mathsf{G3IntQC}
, respectively. Let
\mathcal{R}
be the relational atoms occurring in the relevant rule; the side condition
{\dagger}_{1}
states that
v_{i}\leadsto^{\mathcal{R}}w
for each
i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}
,
{\dagger}_{2}
states that
v_{i}\sim^{\mathcal{R}}w
for each
i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}
,
{\dagger}_{3}
states that
v
is an eigenvariable,
{\dagger}_{4}
states that
v\leadsto^{\mathcal{R}}w
,
{\dagger}_{5}
states that
v\sim^{\mathcal{R}}w
,
{\dagger}_{6}
states that
\underline{a}
is an eigenvariable,
{\dagger}_{7}
states that
v\leadsto^{\mathcal{R}}w
and
\underline{a}
is an eigenvariable, and
{\dagger}_{8}
states that
v\sim^{\mathcal{R}}w
and
\underline{a}
is an eigenvariable.

The next three sections will focus on the non-trivial refinement and translation of our labelled calculi into our nested calculi. As such, we present two useful lemmata below which will aid us in the aforementioned endeavor and allow for us to focus our attention on the refinement and translation from labelled to nested, thus freeing us from being sidetracked by too many auxiliary details. Moreover, we present the rules (mentioned in the abbreviations above and lemmata below) that we expand each labelled calculus with in Fig.
7
below. Some of these rules depend on the notion of a
directed path
or
undirected path
, whose definitions are as follows:

Definition 15
(Directed Path)

Let
\Lambda=\mathcal{R},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta
be a labelled sequent. We say that there exists a
directed path
from
w
to
u
in
\mathcal{R}
(written
w\leadsto^{\mathcal{R}}u
) iff
w=u
, or there exist worlds
v_{i}
(with
i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}
) such that
w\leq v_{1},\ldots,v_{n}\leq u\in\mathcal{R}
holds (we stipulate that
w\leq u\in\mathcal{R}
when
n=0
).

Definition 16
(Undirected Path)

Let
\Lambda=\mathcal{R},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta
be a labelled sequent and
w\sim v\in\{w\leq u,u\leq w\}
. We say that there exists an
undirected path
from
w
to
u
in
\mathcal{R}
(written
w\sim^{\mathcal{R}}u
) iff
w=u
, or there exist worlds
v_{i}
(with
i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}
) such that
w\sim v_{1},\ldots,v_{n}\sim u\in\mathcal{R}
holds (we stipulate that
w\sim u\in\mathcal{R}
when
n=0
).

\mathsf{G3IntQC}

The following lemma is useful in that it explicates what rules freely permute with each other, thus letting us focus only on the non-trivial cases in the sequel.

Lemma 5

The following hold in
\mathsf{G3Int}^{*}
,
\mathsf{G3IntQ}^{*}
, and
\mathsf{G3IntQC}^{*}
:

(i)

The
(ref)
and
(tra)
rules can be permuted above
(id^{*})
,
(\bot_{l})
,
(\wedge_{l})
,
(\wedge_{r})
,
(\vee_{l})
,
(\vee_{r})
,
(\supset_{l}^{*})
,
(\supset_{r})
,
(\neg_{l})
,
(\neg_{r})
,
(ihd)
,
(\exists_{l})
,
(\exists_{r})
, and
(\forall^{c}_{r})
.

(ii)

The
(nd)
,
(cd)
, and
(ihd)
rules can be permuted above
(id)
,
(id^{*})
,
(\bot_{l})
,
(\wedge_{l})
,
(\wedge_{r})
,
(\vee_{l})
,
(\vee_{r})
,
(\supset_{l})
,
(\supset_{l}^{*})
,
(\supset_{r})
,
(\neg_{l})
,
(\neg_{r})
,
(lift)
,
(ihd)
,
(\exists_{l})
,
(\exists^{in}_{r})
,
(\exists^{ic}_{r})
,
(\forall^{in}_{l})
,
(\forall^{ic}_{l})
,
(\forall_{r})
, and
(\forall^{c}_{r})
.

Proof

The claim of (i) follows from the fact that none of the rules mentioned have active relational atoms of the form
w\leq u
in the conclusion, and so,
(ref)
and
(tra)
may be freely permuted above each rule. The claim of (ii) follows from the fact that none of the rules mentioned contain active domain atoms in the conclusion, allowing for
(nd)
,
(cd)
, and
(ihd)
to be permuted above each rule.
∎

5
Deriving the Calculus
\mathsf{NInt}
from
\mathsf{G3Int}

Deriving the calculus
\mathsf{NInt}
from
\mathsf{G3Int}
depends on a crucial observation concerning labelled derivations:
rules such as
(ref)
and
(tra)
allow for theorems to be derived in proofs containing non-treelike labelled sequents
. To demonstrate this fact, observe the following derivation in
\mathsf{G3Int}
:

w\leq v,v\leq v,v:p\Rightarrow v:p

(ref)

w\leq v,v:p\Rightarrow v:p

(\supset_{r})

\Rightarrow w:p\supset p

The initial sequent is non-treelike due to the presence of the
v\leq v
relational atom; however, the application of
(ref)
deletes this structure from the initial sequent and produces a treelike sequent as the conclusion.

In fact, it is true in general that every labelled derivation ending with a treelike sequent can be partitioned into a top derivation consisting of non-treelike sequents, and a bottom derivation consisting of treelike sequents. Note that if a derivation ends with a treelike sequent, then the derivation must necessarily contain a bottom treelike fragment. By contrast, the top non-treelike fragment of the derivation may be empty (e.g. the minimal derivation of
\Rightarrow w:\bot\supset p
).

To demonstrate why the aforementioned partition always exists, suppose you are given a labelled derivation of a treelike sequent and consider the derivation in a bottom-up manner. Observe the each bottom-up application of a rule in
\mathsf{G3Int}
—with the exception of
(ref)
and
(tra)
—will produce a treelike sequent (see Thm.
5.2
for auxiliary details). If, however, at some point in the derivation
(ref)
or
(tra)
is applied, then all sequents above the inference will inherit the (un)directed cycle produced by the rule, thus producing the non-treelike fragment of the proof.

One can therefore imagine that permuting instances of the
(ref)
and
(tra)
rules upward in a given derivation would potentially increase the bottom treelike fragment of the derivation and decrease the top non-treelike fragment. As it so happens, this intuition is correct so long as we choose
adequate
rules—that bottom-up preserve the treelike structure of sequents—to replace certain instances of the
(ref)
and
(tra)
rules in a derivation, when necessary. We will first examine permuting instances of the
(ref)
rule, and motivate which adequate rules we ought to add to our calculus in order to achieve the complete elimination of
(ref)
. After, we will turn our attention toward eliminating the
(tra)
rule, and conclude the section by leveraging our results to show that
\mathsf{NInt}
can be derived from
\mathsf{G3Int}
.

Let us first observe an application of
(ref)
to an initial sequent obtained via the
(id)
rule. There are two possible cases to consider: either the relational atom principal in the initial sequent is active in the
(ref)
inference (shown below left), or it is not (shown below right):

(id)

\mathcal{R},w\leq w,w:p,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:p

(ref)

\mathcal{R},w:p,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:p

(id)

\mathcal{R},u\leq u,w\leq v,w:p,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,v:p

(ref)

\mathcal{R},w\leq v,w:p,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,v:p

In the case shown above right, the end sequent is an instance of the
(id)
rule, regardless of if
u=w
,
u=v
, or
u
is distinct from
w
and
v
. The case shown above left however, indicates that we ought to add the
(id^{*})
rule (see Fig.
7
) to our calculus if we aim to eliminate
(ref)
from any given derivation. These facts, coupled with Lem.
5
, imply that any application of
(ref)
to an initial sequent, produces an initial sequent.

Concerning the remaining rules of
\mathsf{G3Int}
, we need only investigate the permutation of
(ref)
above the
(\supset_{l})
rule, if we rely on Lem.
5
. There are two cases: either the relational atom principal in the
(\supset_{l})
inference is active in the
(ref)
inference, or it is not. The latter case is easily resolved, so we observe the former:

\mathcal{R},w\leq w,w:A\supset B,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:A

\mathcal{R},w\leq w,w:A\supset B,w:B,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

(\supset_{l})

\mathcal{R},w\leq w,w:A\supset B,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

(ref)

\mathcal{R},w:A\supset B,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

Applying
(ref)
to each premise of the
(\supset_{l})
inference yields the following:

\mathcal{R},w\leq w,w:A\supset B,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:A

(ref)

\mathcal{R},w:A\supset B,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:A

\mathcal{R},w\leq w,w:A\supset B,w:B,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

(ref)

\mathcal{R},w:A\supset B,w:B,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

The above observation suggests that we ought to add the
(\supset_{l}^{*})
rule (see Fig.
7
) to our calculus if we wish to permute
(ref)
above the
(\supset_{l})
rule; a single application of the
(\supset_{l}^{*})
rule to the end sequents above gives the desired conclusion.
With the
(\supset_{l}^{*})
rule added to our calculus, we may freely permute the
(ref)
rule above any
(\supset_{l})
inference.

On the basis of our investigation, together with Lem.
5
, we may conclude the following lemma:

Lemma 6

The
(ref)
rule is eliminable in
\mathsf{G3Int}+\{(id^{*}),(\supset^{*}_{l})\}-(tra)
.

Let us turn our attention toward eliminating the
(tra)
rule from a labelled derivation. Since our aim is to eliminate
both

(ref)
and
(tra)
from any derivation, we assume that the rules
\{(id^{*}),(\supset^{*}_{l})\}
have been added to our calculus.

By Lem.
5
,
(tra)
permutes with
(\bot_{l})
and
(id^{*})
, so we only consider the
(id)
case. As with the
(ref)
rule, there are two cases to consider when permuting
(tra)
above an
(id)
inference: either, the active formula of
(tra)
is principal in
(id)
, or it is not. In the latter case, the result of the
(tra)
rule is an initial sequent, implying that the
(tra)
rule may be eliminated from the derivation. The former case proves trickier and is explicitly given below:

(id)

\mathcal{R},w\leq u,u\leq v,w\leq v,w:p,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,v:p

(tra)

\mathcal{R},w\leq u,u\leq v,w:p,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,v:p

Observe that the end sequent is not an initial sequent as it is not obtainable from an
(id)
,
(id^{*})
, or
(\bot_{l})
rule. The issue is solved by considering the
(lift)
rule (see Fig.
7
),
which allows us to obtain the desired end sequent without the use of
(tra)
, as the following derivation demonstrates:

(id^{*})

\mathcal{R},w\leq u,u\leq v,w:p,u:p,v:p,\Gamma\Rightarrow v:p,\Delta

(lift)

\mathcal{R},w\leq u,u\leq v,w:p,u:p,\Gamma\Rightarrow v:p,\Delta

(lift)

\mathcal{R},w\leq u,u\leq v,w:p,\Gamma\Rightarrow v:p,\Delta

Thus, the addition of
(lift)
to our calculus resolves the issue of permuting
(tra)
above any initial sequent. Nevertheless, by Lem.
5
, we still need to consider the permutation of
(tra)
above the
(\supset_{l})
and
(lift)
rules. However, due to the following lemma, we may omit consideration of the
(\supset_{l})
case.

Lemma 7

The rule
(\supset_{l})
is admissible in
\mathsf{G3Int}+\{(id^{*}),(\supset^{*}_{l}),(lift)\}
.

Proof

The derivation below proves the admissibility of the rule:

\mathcal{R},x\leq y,x:A\supset B,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,y:A

(wk)

\mathcal{R},x\leq y,x:A\supset B,y:A\supset B,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,y:A

\mathcal{R},x\leq y,x:A\supset B,y:B,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

(wk)

\mathcal{R},x\leq y,x:A\supset B,y:A\supset B,y:B,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

(\supset^{*}_{l})

\mathcal{R},x\leq y,x:A\supset B,y:A\supset B,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

(lift)

\mathcal{R},x\leq y,x:A\supset B,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

∎

Last, the
(tra)
rule is permutable with the
(lift)
rule. In the case where the principal relational atom of
(lift)
is not active in the ensuing
(tra)
application, the two rules freely permute. The alternative case is resolved as shown below:

\mathcal{R},w\leq u,u\leq v,w\leq v,w:A,v:A,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

(lift)

\mathcal{R},w\leq u,u\leq v,w\leq v,w:A,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

(tra)

\mathcal{R},w\leq u,u\leq v,w:A,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

\mathcal{R},w\leq u,u\leq v,w\leq v,w:A,v:A,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

(tra)

\mathcal{R},w\leq u,u\leq v,w:A,v:A,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

(wk)

\mathcal{R},w\leq u,u\leq v,w:A,u:A,v:A,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

(lift)

\mathcal{R},w\leq u,u\leq v,w:A,u:A,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

(lift)

\mathcal{R},w\leq u,u\leq v,w:A,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

Hence, we obtain the following:

Lemma 8

The
(tra)
rule is eliminable in
\mathsf{G3Int}+\{(id^{*}),(\supset^{*}_{l}),(lift)\}-(ref)
.

Enough groundwork has been laid to state one of our main lemmata, which is also a consequence of the work in
Pim18
.

Lemma 9

The
(ref)
and
(tra)
rules are admissible in the calculus
\mathsf{G3Int}+\{(id^{*}),(\supset^{*}_{l}),(lift)\}
.

Proof

Suppose we are given a derivation in
\mathsf{G3Int}+\{(id^{*}),(\supset^{*}_{l}),(lift)\}
, and consider the topmost occurrence of either
(ref)
or
(tra)
. If we can show that the
(ref)
rule permutes above the
(lift)
rule, then we may invoke Lem.
6
and Lem.
8
to conclude that each topmost occurrence of
(ref)
and
(tra)
can be eliminated from the given derivation in succession. This yields a
(ref)
- and
(tra)
-free proof of the end sequent and establishes the claim. Thus, we prove that the
(ref)
rule permutes above the
(lift)
rule.

In the case where the relational atom active in
(ref)
is not principal in the
(lift)
inference, the two rules may be permuted; the alternative case is resolved as shown below:

\mathcal{R},w\leq w,w:A,w:A,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

(lift)

\mathcal{R},w\leq w,w:A,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

(ref)

\mathcal{R},w:A,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

IH

\mathcal{R},w:A,w:A,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

(ctr_{l})

\mathcal{R},w:A,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

∎

The addition of the rules
\{(id^{*}),(\supset_{l}^{*}),(lift)\}
to our calculus and the above admissibility results demonstrate that we are readily advancing toward our goal of deriving
\mathsf{NInt}
. Howbeit,
our labelled calculus is still distinct since it makes use of the logical signature
\{\bot,\land,\lor,\supset\}
, whereas
\mathsf{NInt}
uses the signature
\{\neg,\land,\lor,\supset\}
. Therefore, we need to show that
(\bot_{l})
(we define
\bot:=p\land\neg p
) is admissible in the presence of (labelled versions of) the
(\neg_{r})
and
(\neg_{l})
rules (see Fig.
7
). This admissibility result is explained in the theorem below.

Theorem 5.1

The rules
\{(id),(\bot_{l}),(\supset_{l}),(ref),(tra)\}
are admissible in
\mathsf{IntL}
.

Proof

Follows from Lem.
5
, Lem.
9
, the fact that
(id)
is derivable using
(id^{*})
and
(lift)
, and the fact that
(\bot_{l})
is derivable from
(\neg_{l})
and
(\wedge_{l})
. Also, the admissibility of
(\supset_{l})
is shown as in Lem.
7
.
∎

Although the above theorem is sufficient to conclude the completeness of
\mathsf{IntL}
, we obtain a stronger result. As shown in the theorem below, we may conclude that
\mathsf{IntL}
is
complete relative to treelike derivations
possessing the
fixed root property
; i.e. for every
\mathsf{Int}
-valid formula
A\in\mathcal{L}
, (i)
\Rightarrow w:A
is derivable in
\mathsf{IntL}
with a treelike derivation, and (ii) the label
w
is the root of each treelike labelled sequent in the derivation.

Theorem 5.2

(i) The calculus
\mathsf{IntL}
is complete relative to treelike derivations with the fixed root property. (ii) Every derivation in
\mathsf{IntL}
of a treelike labelled sequent is a treelike derivation with the fixed root property.

Proof

We prove (i), as (ii) is proven similarly. By Thm.
5.1
above, we know that
\mathsf{IntL}
is complete. To prove claim (i) then, we assume that we are given a derivation in
\mathsf{IntL}
of a labelled theorem, i.e. the end sequent is of the form
\Rightarrow w:A
. It is not difficult to see that the derivation of
\Rightarrow w:A
must be treelike with the fixed root property since applying inference rules from the calculus bottom-up to
\Rightarrow w:A
either preserves relational structure or adds forward relational structure (e.g.
(\supset_{r})
and
(\neg_{r})
), thus constructing a tree emanating from the root
w
.
∎

We may leverage the above theorem and the translation
\mathfrak{N}
(from Def.
11
) to complete the extraction of the nested calculus
\mathsf{NInt}
from the labelled calculus
\mathsf{G3Int}
(via the calculus
\mathsf{IntL}
). The theorem below shows that (the treelike fragment of)
\mathsf{IntL}
and
\mathsf{NInt}
are notational variants of one another:

Theorem 5.3

(i) Every derivation in
\mathsf{IntL}
of a nestedlike labelled sequent
\Lambda
is effectively translatable to a derivation of the nested sequent
\mathfrak{N}(\Lambda)
in
\mathsf{NInt}
. (ii) Every derivation in
\mathsf{NInt}
of a nested sequent
\Sigma
is effectively translatable to a derivation of the labelled sequent
\mathfrak{L}(\Sigma)
in
\mathsf{IntL}
.

Proof

By Lem.
3
, we know that
\Lambda
is treelike, implying that our derivation of
\Lambda
is treelike by Thm.
5.2
, which further implies that the translation function
\mathfrak{N}
is defined for each labelled sequent in the derivation. It is straightforward to verify that each rule in
\mathsf{IntL}
translates to an instance of the corresponding rule in
\mathsf{NInt}
under the
\mathfrak{N}
translation, and every rule of
\mathsf{NInt}
translates to an instance of the corresponding rule in
\mathsf{IntL}
under the
\mathfrak{L}
translation. ∎

6
Deriving the Calculus
\mathsf{NIntQ}
from
\mathsf{G3IntQ}

In the preceding section, we observed that the elimination of the
(ref)
and
(tra)
rules yielded derivations where every labelled sequent was of a treelike shape. In this section (and the succeeding section) the same effect obtains via the elimination of these two structural rules. Therefore, the majority of this section is dedicated to investigating the effects of eliminating the
(nd)
and
(ihd)
structural rules instead.

Similar to our analysis of eliminating the
(ref)
and
(tra)
rules, we motivate and explain the
adequate
rules we ought to add to
\mathsf{G3IntQ}
in order to obtain the complete elimination of
(nd)
and
(ihd)
.
Although the reader may refer to Fig.
7
to witness what rules are needed for the admissibility of
(nd)
and
(ihd)
, a central aim of this section is to demonstrate
how
such rules emerge from our analysis when attempting to eliminate
(nd)
and
(ihd)
from a derivation—this begets a deeper understanding of how the semantics of
\mathsf{IntQ}
affects the shape of rules in
\mathsf{NIntQ}
(via the labelled calculus
\mathsf{G3IntQ}
). Ultimately, our admissibility results will permit the extraction of
\mathsf{NIntQ}
from
\mathsf{G3IntQ}
.

Lemma 10

The
(ref)
and
(tra)
rules are admissible in the calculus
\mathsf{G3IntQ}^{*}
.

Proof

We prove the result by induction on the height of the given derivation and assume w.l.o.g. that the derivation ends with
(ref)
or
(tra)
, and that no other instances of
(ref)
or
(tra)
occur in the derivation. The general result follows by considering a topmost occurrence of
(ref)
or
(tra)
and eliminating each topmost occurrence in succession until a proof free of
(ref)
and
(tra)
inferences is obtained.

By Lem.
5
, we need only show that
(ref)
and
(tra)
permute above the rules
(id_{q}),(id^{n}_{q}),(\supset_{l})
,
(lift)
,
(\exists^{n}_{r})
,
(\exists^{in}_{r})
,
(\forall_{l})
,
(\forall^{n}_{l})
,
(\forall^{in}_{l})
, and
(nd)
. The cases of permuting
(ref)
and
(tra)
above
(lift)
are similar as for Thm.
5.1
and Lem.
8
, respectively. Also,
(\supset_{l})
is admissible in the presence of
(\supset^{*}_{l})
(similar to Lem.
7
),
(id_{q})
is an instance of
(id^{n}_{q})
(by Lem.
11
below), and
(\forall_{l})
is an instance of
(\forall^{n}_{l})
(also by Lem.
11
below), so these cases may be omitted. Hence, we focus only on the nontrivial cases involving the
(id^{n}_{q})
,
(\exists^{n}_{r})
,
(\exists^{in}_{r})
,
(\forall^{n}_{l})
,
(\forall^{in}_{l})
, and
(nd)
rules, which are shown below to the left and resolved as shown below on the right. We prove the elimination of
(ref)
and refer the reader to Appendix
A
for the similar proof of
(tra)
elimination.

Base case.
We let
\mathcal{R}^{\prime}:=\mathcal{R},\underline{a}_{1}\in D_{v_{1}},\ldots,\underline{a}_{n}\in D_{v_{n}}
in the
(id^{n}_{q})
case below. Observe that the end sequent of the derivation below left is an instance of
(id^{n}_{q})
since the side condition that
v_{i}\leadsto^{\mathcal{R}^{\prime}}w
for
i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}
holds: if none of the directed paths from
v_{i}
to
w
contain
u\leq u
, then the paths are present in
\mathcal{R}^{\prime}
, and if a directed path from
v_{i}
to
w
does contain
u\leq u
, then deleting each occurrence of
u\leq u
from the directed path gives a new path from
v_{i}
to
w
in
\mathcal{R}^{\prime}
.

(id^{n}_{q})

We now argue that the side condition (
v\leadsto^{\mathcal{R}}w
) of
(\exists^{n}_{r})
,
(\exists^{in}_{r})
,
(\forall^{n}_{l})
, and
(\forall^{in}_{l})
continues to hold after applying IH above. If the directed path from
v
to
w
does not go through
u
, then the side condition trivially holds. Alternatively, if the directed path from
v
to
w
does go through
u
, then by deleting each occurrence of
u\leq u
from the path, we obtain a new directed path from
v
to
w
, which continues to be present after the invocation of IH.
∎

We now analyze the admissibility of
(nd)
in
\mathsf{G3IntQ}^{*}-\{(ref),(tra)\}
, and afterward, analyze the admissibility of the
(ihd)
rule. It will be instructive to first consider the case of permuting
(nd)
above the
(\exists_{r})
rule solely. It will be seen that in order to permute
(nd)
above
(\exists_{r})
, it is sufficient to strengthen the
(\exists_{r})
rule through the addition of a side condition; this motivates a similar side condition that we will impose on
(id_{q})
(yielding the rule
(id^{n}_{q})
) and on
(\forall_{l})
(yielding the rule
(\forall^{n}_{l})
).

To begin our analysis, observe (1) a non-trivial application of
(nd)
after an
(\exists_{r})
inference, and (2) the result of applying
(nd)
to the top sequent in (1).

\mathcal{R},v\leq w,\underline{a}\in D_{v},\underline{a}\in D_{w},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:A(\underline{a}/x),w:\exists xA

(\exists_{r})

\mathcal{R},v\leq w,\underline{a}\in D_{v},\underline{a}\in D_{w},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:\exists xA

(nd)

\mathcal{R},v\leq w,\underline{a}\in D_{v},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:\exists xA

(1)

\mathcal{R},v\leq w,\underline{a}\in D_{v},\underline{a}\in D_{w},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:A(\underline{a}/x),w:\exists xA

(nd)

\mathcal{R},v\leq w,\underline{a}\in D_{v},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:A(\underline{a}/x),w:\exists xA

(2)

In (2), the application of
(nd)
has generated a labelled sequent where the domain atom (i.e.
\underline{a}\in D_{v}
) is associated with the label
v

one step in the past
of
w
(due to the presence of the
v\leq w
relational atom). One possible solution to overcome this obstacle, and to allow for the permutation of
(nd)
above
(\exists_{r})
, would be to add the following rule to our calculus:

\mathcal{R},v\leq w,\underline{a}\in D_{v},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:A(\underline{a}/x),w:\exists xA

(\exists_{r})^{\prime}

\mathcal{R},v\leq w,\underline{a}\in D_{v},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:\exists xA

In the rule above, the domain atom
\underline{a}\in D_{v}
is associated with the label
v
, which is
one step in the past
of
w
. Although the addition of the above rule solves the problem of permuting
(nd)
above the
(\exists_{r})
rule, its inclusion into our calculus would inevitably place us in a similar, undesirable circumstance:

\mathcal{R},u\leq v,v\leq w,\underline{a}\in D_{u},\underline{a}\in D_{v},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:A(\underline{a}/x),w:\exists xA

(\exists_{r})^{\prime}

\mathcal{R},u\leq v,v\leq w,\underline{a}\in D_{u},\underline{a}\in D_{v},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:\exists xA

(nd)

\mathcal{R},u\leq v,v\leq w,\underline{a}\in D_{u},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:\exists xA

\mathcal{R},u\leq v,v\leq w,\underline{a}\in D_{u},\underline{a}\in D_{v},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:A(\underline{a}/x),w:\exists xA

(nd)

\mathcal{R},u\leq v,v\leq w,\underline{a}\in D_{u},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:A(\underline{a}/x),w:\exists xA

It appears that now we would need to add a new version of the
(\exists_{r})
rule allowing us to delete
w:A(\underline{a})
when the required relational atom
\underline{a}\in D_{u}
is associated with a label (viz.
u
) that is
two steps in the past
of
w
(due to the occurrence of
u\leq v,v\leq w
). Including such a rule however, would inevitably force us to add another existential rule where the required relational atom is associated with a label
three steps in the past
—such rule inclusions would then continue ad infinitum. To resolve the problem, and capture all such possibilities, we add the following rule to our calculus, which has the side condition
v\leadsto^{\mathcal{R}}w
(see Def.
15
and Fig.
7
):

\mathcal{R},\underline{a}\in D_{v},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:A(\underline{a}/x),w:\exists xA

(\exists^{n}_{r})

\mathcal{R},\underline{a}\in D_{v},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:\exists xA

This rule generalizes the shifting behaviour of the domain atom witnessed above to include all possible
shifts
.
Furthermore, due to the fact that the labelled sequents we are considering encode an
\mathsf{IntQ}
-model—which satisfies the
nested domain
condition—it is appropriate to impose the above side condition, which essentially states that
if an object is an element of some domain
D_{v}
in the past of
w
, then it is an element of the domain
D_{w}
. It is straightforward to verify that the
(\exists^{n}_{r})
rule is sound relative to
\mathsf{IntQ}
-models.

If one analyzes the cases of permuting
(nd)
above the
(id_{q})
and
(\forall_{l})

(\exists_{r})

(id_{q})
and
(\forall_{l})
to obtain the
(id^{n}_{q})
and
(\forall^{n}_{l})

Lemma 11

The
(id_{q})

(\exists_{r})
, and
(\forall_{l})
rules are instances of the
(id^{n}_{q})
,
(\exists^{n}_{r})
, and
(\forall^{n}_{l})
rules, respectively.

Lemma 12

\mathsf{G3IntQ}^{*}-\{(ref),(tra)\}

We now turn our attention toward analyzing the admissibility of

\mathcal{R},\Gamma,w:\forall xA,\Rightarrow\Delta

where we impose the side condition that

and
\underline{a}

inhabited

Lemma 13

The rule
(ihd)
is admissible in
\mathsf{G3IntQ}^{*}-\{(ref),(tra),(nd)\}
.

Proof

We prove the result by induction on the height of the given derivation. The base case is simple as any application of
(ihd)
to
(id^{n}_{q})
or
(\bot_{l})
yields another instance of the rule. By Lem.

and Lem.

, the only cases we need to consider in the inductive step are the non-trivial

and
(\forall^{n}_{l})
cases; however, as we saw above, the non-trivial cases can be handled by applying
(\exists^{in}_{r})
or
(\forall^{in}_{l})
, respectively.

Although the above theorem is fundamental for translating derivations in
\mathsf{IntQL}
into derivations in
\mathsf{NIntQ}
, additional work needs to be done to ensure that the
(\exists^{n}_{r})
and
(\forall^{n}_{l})
rules properly translate to instances of the
(\exists_{r})
and
(\forall_{l})
rules. The side condition imposed on
(\exists^{n}_{r})
and
(\forall^{n}_{l})
relies on the existence of a domain atom containing a parameter
\underline{a}
, whereas the side condition imposed on the nested
(\exists_{r})
and
(\forall_{l})
rules stipulates that the parameter
\underline{a}
must either be an eigenvariable or available. The question arises: how do we reconcile these seemingly distinct side conditions?

Interestingly, our process of refinement has offered us an unadulterated perspective of the nested
(\exists_{r})
and
(\forall_{l})
rules. As will be argued below (Thm.
6.3
), the rules
(\exists^{in}_{r})
and
(\forall^{in}_{l})
in
\mathsf{IntQL}
translate to instances of the nested
(\exists_{r})
and
(\forall_{l})
rules where the relevant parameter of the inference is an
eigenvariable
, and the rules
(\exists^{n}_{r})
and
(\forall^{n}_{l})
translate to instances of the nested
(\exists_{r})
and
(\forall_{l})
rules where the relevant parameter of the inference is
available
. In other words, what are single rules with a disjunctive side condition in the nested setting have bifurcated into distinct sets of rules with atomic side conditions in the labelled setting.

In order to ensure that instances of
(\exists^{n}_{r})
and
(\forall^{n}_{l})
properly translate to instances of the nested
(\exists_{r})
and
(\forall_{l})
rules then, we must show that if the side condition of the former rules holds, then the side condition of the latter rules holds. This motivates the definition of a
nested form
derivation:

Definition 17
(Nested Form)

Let
\Pi
be a derivation of a labelled sequent
\Lambda
in
\mathsf{IntQL}
. We define
\Pi
to be in
nested form
iff (i)
\Lambda
is nestedlike, and (ii) for each instance of
(\exists^{n}_{r})
and
(\forall^{n}_{l})
in
\Pi
:

\mathcal{R},\underline{a}\in D_{v},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:A(\underline{a}/x),w:\exists xA

(\exists^{n}_{r})

\mathcal{R},\underline{a}\in D_{v},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:\exists xA

\mathcal{R},\underline{a}\in D_{v},w:A(\underline{a}/x),w:\forall xA,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

(\forall^{n}_{l})

\mathcal{R},\underline{a}\in D_{v},w:\forall xA,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

there exists a formula
u:B(\underline{a})
such that
u\leadsto^{\mathcal{R}}w
in the conclusion of the inference.

Assuming we are given a nested form derivation in
\mathsf{IntQL}
, condition (ii) of the above definition ensures that instances of
(\exists^{n}_{r})
and
(\forall^{n}_{l})
will properly translate into instances of
(\exists_{r})
and
(\forall_{l})
in
\mathsf{NIntQ}
. Additionally, nested form proofs are significant because one can view the space of nested form proofs in
\mathsf{IntQL}
as being equivalent to the space of proofs generated by
\mathsf{NIntQ}
, as confirmed by Thm.
6.3
and
6.4
below. Before we establish this correspondence however, the following lemma is needed for the proof of Thm.
6.3
, that is, for showing that if a nestedlike labelled sequent
\Lambda
is provable in
\mathsf{IntQL}
, then
\mathfrak{N}(\Lambda)
is provable in
\mathsf{NIntQ}
.

Lemma 14

If a nestedlike labelled sequent
\Lambda
is derivable in
\mathsf{IntQL}
, then
\Lambda
has a nested form derivation in
\mathsf{IntQL}
.

The truth of the above lemma can be seen to follow from Thm.
6.4
below (which states that each derivation in
\mathsf{NIntQ}
of a nested sequent
\Sigma
can be translated into a nested form derivation of
\mathfrak{L}(\Sigma)
in
\mathsf{IntQL}
) in conjunction with a few facts: (i)
\mathsf{IntQL}
is sound, (ii) one can show by semantic arguments that if a nestedlike labelled sequent
\Lambda
is valid, then so is
\mathfrak{N}(\Lambda)
, (iii) by Fitting’s work in
Fit14
, we know that
\mathsf{NIntQ}
is strongly complete (Thm.
3.2
), and (iv) for any nestedlike labelled sequent
\Lambda
,
\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{N}(\Lambda))=\Lambda
(Lem.
3
).
4
4

4

The soundness of
\mathsf{IntQL}
is established by Thm.
8.1
in Sect.
8
, where it is shown that every derivation in
\mathsf{IntQL}
can be effectively transformed into a derivation of the same labelled sequent in
\mathsf{G3IntQ}
. Since
\mathsf{G3IntQ}
is sound by Thm.
3.1
, this establishes the soundness of
\mathsf{IntQL}
.
Hence, given a derivable nestedlike labelled sequent
\Lambda
, which is therefore valid since
\mathsf{IntQL}
is sound by (i), it follows that
\mathfrak{N}(\Lambda)
is valid by (ii), meaning that
\mathfrak{N}(\Lambda)
is derivable by (iii), and so by Thm.
6.4
below,
\mathfrak{L}(\mathfrak{N}(\Lambda))
has a nested form derivation, i.e.
\Lambda
has a nested form derivation by (iv). Although this argument serves as a proof of Lem.
14
, it is not entirely satisfactory.

The above argument relies on the completeness of
\mathsf{NIntQ}
, and so, if our aim were to extract
\mathsf{NIntQ}
from
\mathsf{G3IntQ}
without any prior knowledge of
\mathsf{NIntQ}
or its properties, or to show
\mathsf{NIntQ}
complete via this extraction, then since the above argument relies on the completeness of
\mathsf{NIntQ}
(i.e. Thm.
3.2
), we would fail to reach our aim. The author sees at least two possible strategies for confirming the above lemma without relying on the completeness of
\mathsf{NIntQ}
. In the first method, one could write a (potentially non-terminating) proof-search procedure for
\mathsf{IntQL}
that takes a nestedlike labelled sequent
\Lambda
as input and attempts to construct a nested form proof of
\Lambda
, showing that a counter-model for
\Lambda
can be constructed given that the procedure does not halt with a nested form proof of the input. Such a method of proof would effectively prove the completeness of
\mathsf{IntQL}
relative to valid nestedlike labelled sequents while showing that every such sequent possesses a nested form proof. The second method consists of showing how to algorithmically transform any derivation of a nestedlike labelled sequent
\Lambda
in
\mathsf{IntQL}
into a nested form proof of
\Lambda
. Such methods of proof are desirable as they would effectively demonstrate that
\mathsf{NIntQ}
inherits completeness from its associated labelled calculus
\mathsf{G3IntQ}
, however, we leave such results to future work, and continue our investigation of the correspondence between semantic and nested systems.

(\exists^{in}_{r})
