, which,
ipso facto
, makes the conclusion a nestedlike labelled sequent; hence, the derivation satisfies property (i) of Def.
17
. Second, observe that the output derivation in
\mathsf{IntQL}
satisfies property (ii) of Def.
17
since each
(\exists^{n}_{r})
and
(\forall^{n}_{r})
inference is obtained from an
(\exists_{r})
or
(\forall_{l})
inference in the input derivation, ensuring the existence of a labelled formula
u:B(\underline{a})
in the conclusion of any
(\exists^{n}_{r})
or
(\forall^{n}_{r})
inference such that there is a directed path from
u
to the label
w
prefixing the principal formula.
∎

7
Deriving the Calculus
\mathsf{NIntQC}
from
\mathsf{G3IntQC}

In the previous section, we saw that strengthening the
(\exists_{r})
and
(\forall_{l})
rules allowed for the rules
(nd)
and
(ihd)
to be eliminated from any given derivation. In this section, we will focus on how to strengthen these rules even further to additionally obtain the elimination of
(cd)
from any given derivation. We begin our analysis after first stating the following admissibility result:

Lemma 15

The
(ref)
and
(tra)
rules are admissible in the calculus
\mathsf{G3IntQC}^{*}
.

Proof

The proof is similar to Lem.
10
and is detailed in Appendix
A
for the interested reader.
∎

The exclusion of
(ref)
and
(tra)
implies the completeness of
\mathsf{G3IntQC}^{*}-\{(ref),(tra)\}
relative to treelike derivations, similar to Lem.
6.2
. We therefore assume for the rest of the section that all labelled sequents we consider are treelike—this assumption will ease our admissibility analyses of
(nd)
,
(cd)
, and
(ihd)
, though note that the assumption can be omitted, if desired.

Previously, we saw that permutations of the
(nd)
rule above the
(id_{q})
,
(\exists_{r})
, and
(\forall_{l})
rules shifted domain atoms to the past. We now investigate how permutations of the
(cd)
rule affect domain atoms in
(id_{q})
,
(\exists_{r})
, and
(\forall_{l})
. As before, we first concentrate on permuting
(cd)
above the
(\exists_{r})
rule solely. Observing the effect of permuting
(cd)
above
(\exists_{r})
will motivate how we strengthen the rule—and the
(id_{q})
and
(\forall_{l})
rules—to obtain the complete elimination of
(cd)
from any given derivation.

To begin our analysis, observe (3) a non-trivial application of
(cd)
after an
(\exists_{r})
inference, and (4) the result of applying
(cd)
to the top sequent in (3).

\mathcal{R},w\leq v,\underline{a}\in D_{w},\underline{a}\in D_{v},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:A(\underline{a}/x),w:\exists xA

(\exists_{r})

\mathcal{R},w\leq v,\underline{a}\in D_{w},\underline{a}\in D_{v},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:\exists xA

(cd)

\mathcal{R},w\leq v,\underline{a}\in D_{v},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:\exists xA

(3)

\mathcal{R},w\leq v,\underline{a}\in D_{w},\underline{a}\in D_{v},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:A(\underline{a}/x),w:\exists xA

(cd)

\mathcal{R},w\leq v,\underline{a}\in D_{v},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:A(\underline{a}/x),w:\exists xA

(4)

The application of
(cd)
has generated a labelled sequent where the domain atom (i.e.
\underline{a}\in D_{v}
) is associated with the label
v

one step in the future
of
w
(due to the presence of the
w\leq v
relational atom). By analogy to what we saw in the last section (in the case of permuting
(nd)
above
(\exists_{r})
), it is not hard to see that successive (non-trivial) permutations of
(cd)
above an
(\exists_{r})
inference will continually shift the domain atom to the future. If—at the same time—we also consider (non-trivial) permutations of the
(nd)
rule above the
(\exists_{r})
rule, then the domain atom can shift either to the future or the past.

Recall that we have restricted our analysis to only consider derivations in
\mathsf{G3IntQC}^{*}-\{(ref),(tra)\}
that employ treelike labelled sequents. Observe that
any node
in the graph of a treelike labelled sequent is reachable from any other node by a sequence of forward and backwards edges. This property of treelike labelled sequents, accompanied by the witnessed shifting behavior discussed in the previous paragraph, suggests that we ought to add the following
(\exists^{c}_{r})
rule (see Fig.
7
) to our calculus:

\mathcal{R},\underline{a}\in D_{v},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:A(\underline{a}/x),w:\exists xA

(\exists^{c}_{r})

\mathcal{R},\underline{a}\in D_{v},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:\exists xA

with the side condition that
v\sim^{\mathcal{R}}w
, i.e. there is an undirected path from the label
v
to the label
w
. Observe that this side condition generalizes the shifting behaviour of the domain atom to include all possible forward and backward
shifts
. Intuitively, this side condition states that
if an object is an element of some domain
D_{v}
, then it is an element of the domain
D_{w}
, which always holds in the
constant domain
setting.

The same shifting behavior can be witnessed by considering the permutation of
(nd)
and
(cd)
above the
(id_{q})
and
(\forall_{l})
rules. Thus, we strengthen those rules in a similar way to obtain the
(id^{c}_{q})
and
(\forall^{c}_{l})
rules (see Fig.
7
).

Lemma 16

The
(id_{q})
,
(\exists_{r})
, and
(\forall_{l})
rules are instances of the
(id^{c}_{q})
,
(\exists^{c}_{r})
, and
(\forall^{c}_{l})
rules, respectively.

The lemma below confirms that the strengthened versions of
(id_{q})
,
(\exists_{r})
, and
(\forall_{l})
are sufficient to prove the admissibility of the
(nd)
and
(cd)
rules in the calculus
\mathsf{G3IntQC}^{*}-\{(ref),(tra)\}
:

Lemma 17

The rules
(nd)
and
(cd)
are admissible in the calculus
\mathsf{G3IntQC}^{*}-\{(ref),(tra)\}
.

Proof

The proof is similar to the proof of Lem.
12
, but where undirected paths (Def.
16
) are used instead of directed paths (Def.
15
).
∎

In the previous section, we saw that permutations of
(ihd)
above the
(\exists^{n}_{r})
and
(\forall^{n}_{l})
rules could not be performed in certain cases. To resolve this issue, we introduced versions of the rules that absorbed the
(ihd)
rule. The same phenomenon occurs in the case of the
(\exists^{c}_{r})
and
(\forall^{c}_{l})
rules, implying that we need to add
(\exists^{ic}_{r})
and
(\forall^{ic}_{l})
to our calculus (see Fig.
7
).

Lemma 18

The rule
(ihd)
is admissible in
\mathsf{G3IntQC}^{*}-\{(ref),(tra),(nd),(cd)\}
.

Proof

Similar to the proof of Lem.
13
.
∎

Theorem 7.1

The rules
(id_{q})
,
(\bot_{l})
,
(\supset_{l})
,
(ref)
,
(tra)
,
(\exists_{r}),(\forall_{l})
,
(\forall_{r})
,
(nd)
,
(cd)
, and
(ihd)
are admissible in the calculus
\mathsf{IntQCL}
.

Proof

The admissibility of
\{(ref),(tra)\}
,
\{(id_{q}),(\exists_{r}),(\forall_{l})\}
,
\{(nd),(cd)\}
, and
(ihd)
follow from Lem.
15
, Lem.
16
, Lem.
17
, and Lem.
18
, respectively. Admissibility of
(\supset_{l})
and
(\bot_{l})
is shown as stated in Thm.
6.1
. Admissibility of
(\forall_{r})
in the presence of
(\forall^{c}_{r})
is shown below:

\mathcal{R},w\leq v,\underline{a}\in D_{v},\Gamma\Rightarrow v:A(\underline{a}/x),\Delta

(lsub)

\mathcal{R},w\leq w,\underline{a}\in D_{w},\Gamma\Rightarrow w:A(\underline{a}/x),\Delta

(ref)

\mathcal{R},\underline{a}\in D_{w},\Gamma\Rightarrow w:A(\underline{a}/x),\Delta

Theorem 7.2

(i) The calculus
\mathsf{IntQCL}
is complete relative to treelike derivations with the fixed root property. (ii) Every derivation in
\mathsf{IntQCL}
of a treelike labelled sequent is a treelike derivation with the fixed root property.

Proof

Similar to Thm.
5.2
.
∎

Although we relied on the notion of a nested form derivation (Def.
17
) in the previous section to translate proofs from the refined labelled calculus
\mathsf{IntQL}
into proofs in the nested calculus
\mathsf{NIntQ}
, we note that this notion, or an analog thereof, is unnecessary to translate derivations from
\mathsf{IntQCL}
to
\mathsf{NIntQC}
. This follows from the fact that side conditions are not imposed on
(\exists_{r})
and
(\forall_{l})
in
\mathsf{NIntQC}
—contrary to what is the case in
\mathsf{NIntQ}
. Hence, applications of
(\exists^{c}_{r})
and
(\forall^{c}_{l})
in
\mathsf{IntQCL}
need not satisfy certain condition in order to be translated, thus simplifying the translation from labelled to nested in the constant domain setting.

Theorem 7.3

Every derivation in
\mathsf{IntQCL}
of a nestedlike labelled sequent
\Lambda
is effectively translatable to a derivation of the nested sequent
\mathfrak{N}(\Lambda)
in
\mathsf{NIntQC}
.

Proof

By Lem.
3
, we know that
\Lambda
is treelike, implying that the derivation of
\Lambda
is treelike by Thm.
7.2
, and so, the translation function
\mathfrak{N}
is defined. When translating from labelled to nested, the existential rules
(\exists^{c}_{r})
and
(\exists^{ic}_{r})
, and the universal rules
(\forall^{c}_{l})
and
(\forall^{ic}_{l})
, translate to instances of
(\exists_{r})
and
(\forall_{l})
, respectively. All remaining rules in
\mathsf{IntQCL}
translate to their corresponding version in the nested calculus.
∎

Theorem 7.4

Every derivation in
\mathsf{NIntQC}
of a nested sequent
\Sigma
is effectively translatable to a derivation of the labelled sequent
\mathfrak{L}(\Sigma)
in
\mathsf{IntQCL}
.

Proof

We show how to translate an instance of
(\exists_{r})
; the remaining cases are similar to those in the proof of Thm.
6.3
. Suppose we aim to translate an
(\exists_{r})
inference occurring in our input derivation:

\Sigma\{X\rightarrow A(\underline{a}/x),\exists xA,Y\}

(\exists_{r})

\Sigma\{X\rightarrow\exists xA,Y\}

If the parameter
\underline{a}
in the above inference is an eigenvariable, then we translate the inference to an instance of
(\exists^{in}_{r})
in
\mathsf{IntQCL}
. However, if the parameter occurs in a side formula, then the translation is non-trivial. Suppose then, that there exists some formula
B(\underline{a})
(different than the occurrence of
A(\underline{a}/x)
) occurring in the premise of the
(\exists_{r})
inference above. Suppose that the translation
\mathfrak{L}
assigns the label
u
to all formulae in the component where
B(\underline{a})
occurs, and note that
u:B(\underline{a})\in\Gamma,\Delta
below. This, in conjunction with the definition of
\mathfrak{L}
(Def.
12
), implies the existence of a domain atom
\underline{a}\in D_{u}
in the image of
\Sigma\{X\rightarrow A(\underline{a}/x),\exists xA,Y\}
under
\mathfrak{L}
(which is explicitly included in the derivation below). Since
\mathfrak{L}(\Sigma\{X\rightarrow A(\underline{a}/x),\exists xA,Y\})
is a treelike labelled sequent, there must exist an undirected path
u\sim v_{1}
,
\ldots
,
v_{n}\sim w
from
u
to
w
in
\mathcal{R}
, i.e.
u\sim^{\mathcal{R}}w
. (NB. If
u=w
, then the translation is straightforward, so we omit consideration of that case.) If we weaken in domain atoms of the form
\underline{a}\in D_{v_{i}}
(with
i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}
) along this undirected path, invoke the admissibility of
(nd)
and
(cd)
(Thm.
7.1
), and then apply
(\exists^{c}_{r})
, we obtain the image of the conclusion of the
(\exists_{r})
inference above under the
\mathfrak{L}
translation. This entire process is succinctly demonstrated in the derivation below:

\mathfrak{L}(\Sigma\{X\rightarrow A(\underline{a}/x),\exists xA,Y\})

.
=

\mathcal{R},\underline{a}\in D_{u},\underline{a}\in D_{w},\Gamma\Rightarrow w:A(\underline{a}/x),w:\exists xA,\Delta

(wk)

\mathcal{R},\underline{a}\in D_{u},\underline{a}\in D_{v_{1}},\ldots,\underline{a}\in D_{v_{n}},\underline{a}\in D_{w},\Gamma\Rightarrow w:A(\underline{a}/x),w:\exists xA,\Delta

(nd)\times k_{1}+(cd)\times k_{2}

\mathcal{R},\underline{a}\in D_{u},\Gamma\Rightarrow w:A(\underline{a}/x),w:\exists xA,\Delta

(\exists^{c}_{r})

\mathcal{R},\underline{a}\in D_{u},\Gamma\Rightarrow w:\exists xA,\Delta

.
=

\mathfrak{L}(\Sigma\{X\rightarrow\exists xA,Y\})

Note that
k_{1}+k_{2}=n+1
, i.e.
k_{1}+k_{2}
is the number of labels occurring in the undirected path from
u
to
w
occurring after
u
and including
w
.
∎

8
Reverse Translations, Corollaries, and Inheritance

The previous three sections were dedicated to refining the labelled calculi
\mathsf{G3Int}
,
\mathsf{G3IntQ}
, and
\mathsf{G3IntQC}
to obtain refined labelled variants that were translatable into nested calculi. In this section, we analyze and provide the reverse translations from
\mathsf{NInt}
,
\mathsf{NIntQ}
, and
\mathsf{NIntQC}
to
\mathsf{G3Int}
,
\mathsf{G3IntQ}
, and
\mathsf{G3IntQC}
, respectively. These reverse translations are interesting in that they demonstrate how to add further syntactic structures and semantic information in order to obtain the more complicated semantic systems from the more refined nested systems. Additionally, these reverse translations can be leveraged to show that each nested calculus inherits proof theoretic properties from each labelled calculus, which we discuss in the second subsection.

8.1
Reverse Translations

When translating from labelled to nested, we discovered what new rules and what strengthened versions of rules were needed in order to allow the elimination of certain structural rules (e.g.
(ref)
and
(nd)
) from a derivation. Obtaining the reverse translation is much simpler, as we already know what rules need to be shown admissible. Lem.
19
–
21
below show how to effectively transform derivations from
\mathsf{IntL}
,
\mathsf{IntQL}
, and
\mathsf{IntQCL}
into
\mathsf{G3Int}
,
\mathsf{G3IntQ}
, and
\mathsf{G3IntQC}
, respectively. These transformations, coupled with the translations from Thm.
5.3
,
6.4
, and
7.4
, yield effective translations from our nested calculi to the
\mathsf{G3}
-style labelled calculi.

Lemma 19
(
Pim18
)

The rules
(id^{*})
,
(\supset_{l}^{*})
, and
(lift)
are admissible in
\mathsf{G3Int}
.

Proof

The proof of the admissibility of each rule in
\mathsf{G3Int}
is shown below:

\mathcal{R},w\leq w,\Gamma,w:p\Rightarrow w:p,\Delta

(ref)

\mathcal{R},\Gamma,w:p\Rightarrow w:p,\Delta

\mathcal{R},w:A\supset B,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:A

(wk)

\mathcal{R},w\leq w,w:A\supset B,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta,w:A

\mathcal{R},w:A\supset B,w:B,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

(wk)

\mathcal{R},w\leq w,w:A\supset B,w:B,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

(\supset_{l})

\mathcal{R},w\leq w,w:A\supset B,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

(ref)

\mathcal{R},w:A\supset B,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

Thm.

-(i)-(a)

\mathcal{R},w\leq v,\Gamma,w:A\Rightarrow v:A,\Delta

8.2
Corollaries and Inheritance

An appealing consequence of our refinement and translation procedures is that our nested calculi inherit desirable proof-theoretic properties from their associated labelled calculi. Such properties are stated in Cor.
1
–
4
below.

As mentioned near the end of Sect.
6
, the translation of proofs from
\mathsf{IntQL}
into proofs in
\mathsf{NIntQ}
(Thm.
6.3
) relies on the completeness of the latter (Thm.
3.2
); hence, we are barred from leveraging this proof-theoretic translation to conclude that
\mathsf{NIntQ}
ultimately inherits completeness from
\mathsf{G3IntQ}
. (NB. In Sect.
6
, we also discussed methods of proof that would free us from relying on the completeness of
\mathsf{NIntQ}
, thus allowing for this inheritance result to go through.) Nevertheless, this issue does not arise in our work concerning propositional intuitionistic logic
\mathsf{Int}
and first-order intuitionistic logic with constant domains
\mathsf{IntQC}
, and so, we may conclude the following corollary:

Corollary 1

The calculi
\mathsf{NInt}
and
\mathsf{NIntQC}
have inherited soundness and completeness from
\mathsf{G3Int}
and
\mathsf{G3IntQC}
, respectively.

Proof

Soundness follows from Thm.
3.1
and
8.2
. Regarding completeness, observe that if
A
is a theorem of
\mathsf{Int}
or
\mathsf{IntQC}
, then
\vec{a}\in D_{w}\Rightarrow w:A
is derivable in
\mathsf{G3Int}
or
\mathsf{G3IntQC}
(respectively) by Thm.
3.1
. By Thm.
5.1
and
5.3
, or Thm.
7.1
and
7.3
, the derivation of
\vec{a}\in D_{w}\Rightarrow w:A
may be transformed and translated into a derivation of
A
in
\mathsf{NInt}
or
\mathsf{NIntQC}
, respectively.
∎

Furthermore, we obtain the admissibility of the set of structural rules presented in Fig.

. This set of structural rules was primarily identified by investigating the variety of ways in which labelled structural rules (e.g.
(wk)

(ctr_{r})

2

for the interested reader.

All rules in
\mathrm{NR}

\mathsf{NInt}
,
\mathsf{NIntQ}
and
\mathsf{NIntQC}

All rules in

(mrg_{2})
, we can show that each derivation in
\mathsf{NIntQ}

Corollary 5

(i) Every derivation in
\mathsf{IntQL}
is transformable into a derivation in
\mathsf{IntQCL}
. (ii) Every derivation in
\mathsf{NIntQ}
is transformable into a derivation in
\mathsf{NIntQC}
.

Proof

Observe that the
(\exists^{n}_{r})
,
(\exists^{in}_{r})
,
(\forall^{n}_{l})
, and
(\forall^{in}_{l})
rules in
\mathsf{IntQL}
are instances of the
(\exists^{c}_{r})
,
(\exists^{ic}_{r})
,
(\forall^{c}_{l})
, and
(\forall^{ic}_{l})
rules in
\mathsf{IntQCL}
. Additionally, the same relationship holds true of the
(\exists_{r})
and
(\forall_{l})
rules in
\mathsf{NIntQ}
and
\mathsf{NIntQC}
. Thus, the only rules that differ between the systems
\mathsf{IntQL}
and
\mathsf{IntQCL}
are the
(\forall_{r})
and
(\forall^{c}_{r})
rules, and the only rules that differ between the systems

and
\mathsf{NIntQC}
are the
(\forall^{n}_{r})
and
(\forall^{c}_{r})
rules. Therefore, we show below that
(\forall_{r})
and
(\forall^{n}_{r})
are admissible in
\mathsf{IntQCL}
and
\mathsf{NIntQC}
, respectively, which proves the claim since all remaining cases are straightforward.

9
Conclusion

In this paper, we mapped out the interrelationships between semantic systems and Fitting’s nested calculi for intuitionistic logics. We focused extensively on
how
to eliminate the structural rules of the labelled calculi
\mathsf{G3Int}
,
\mathsf{G3IntQ}
, and
\mathsf{G3IntQC}
from derivations, by considering how to strengthen their logical rules, or via the addition of new rules. We referred to this process as the method of
refinement
since it ultimately yielded the more refined (sound and complete) calculi
\mathsf{IntL}
,
\mathsf{IntQL}
, and
\mathsf{IntQCL}
which omitted the use of semantically explicit structural rules (e.g.
(ref)
and
(nd)
) and only required treelike labelled sequents in derivations. We saw that fragments of these refined labelled calculi were equivalent to Fitting’s nested calculi
Fit14
. Moreover, we also observed that Fitting’s nested calculi inherited proof-theoretic properties from their associated labelled calculi; e.g. soundness and completeness, invertibility of rules, and admissibility of
(cut)
. Such results suggest that structural rule elimination is a natural method for connecting the relational semantics of a logic to a nested calculus for the logic (via the labelled sequent paradigm).

The method of refining labelled calculi into nested calculi for intuitionistic logics is part of a larger project that seeks to investigate the extent to which such refinements can be performed. Due to general results concerning the construction of labelled calculi, their modularity, and the confirmation of their proof-theoretic properties
CiaMafSpe13
;
DycNeg12
;
Gab96
;
Sim94
, the exposition of a method for deriving refined (or, nested) calculi—which utilize sequents with a simpler underlying data structure (e.g. trees) and have proven to be well-suited for certain automated reasoning tasks (e.g. proof-search
TiuIanGor12
, counter-model extraction
LyoBer19
;
TiuIanGor12
, and effective interpolation
LyoTiuGorClo20
)—from semantic systems could prove to be of practical consequence. Moreover, since labelled calculi are easily obtained from a logic’s semantics, the method of refinement provides a means by which (nested) proof calculi with favorable properties may be obtained directly from a logic’s semantics.

Work funded by FWF projects I2982 and W1255-N23.

Proof

We argue that properties (i)–(v) obtain for
\mathsf{G3IntQC}
; by omitting consideration of the
(cd)
rule, we obtain proofs of these properties for
\mathsf{G3IntQ}
as well.

Claim (i).
Claims (a) and (b) are shown in
(
DycNeg12
, Lem. 1)
, so we focus on proving (c) and (d). We prove claims (c) and (d) together by mutual induction on the complexity of
A
.

Claim (i)-(c).
The base case is resolved using the
(id_{q})
rule for atomic formulae and the
(\bot_{l})
rule for
\bot
. We provide the cases for
\supset
,
\exists
, and
\forall
for the inductive step; the
\lor
and
\land
cases are simple to verify. Note that for the
\supset
case the parameters

\mkern 2.0mu\textstyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\textstyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr

\hfil\textstyle\underline{a}_{1}\hfil

and

\mkern 2.0mu\textstyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\textstyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr

\hfil\textstyle\underline{a}_{2}\hfil

are all and only those parameters that occur in

\mkern 2.0mu\textstyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\textstyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr

\hfil\textstyle\underline{a}\hfil

, with

\mkern 2.0mu\textstyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\textstyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr

\hfil\textstyle\underline{a}_{1}\hfil

and

\mkern 2.0mu\textstyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\textstyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr

\hfil\textstyle\underline{a}_{2}\hfil

potentially intersecting. Also, the

Claim (i)-(d).
The base case for atomic formulae is shown below; the case for
\bot
is omitted as it is simple to verify using the
(\bot_{l})
rule. We provide the
\supset
,
\exists
, and
\forall
cases as the cases for the other connectives are straightforward to prove.

Claim (ii).
We consider two sets of rules from
\mathrm{LR}
in turn.

The
\{(lsub),(psub)\}
rules.
Hp-admissibility of
(lsub)
and
(psub)
are proven by induction on the height of the given derivation; both are similar to
(
DycNeg12
, Lem. 3)
. The only non-trivial cases for the former are the
(\supset_{r})
and
(\forall_{r})
rules of the inductive step, and the non-trivial cases for the latter are the
(\exists_{l})
,
(\forall_{r})
, and
(ihd)
rules of the inductive step. In such cases, the side condition must be preserved if the rule is to be applied. Nevertheless, this can be ensured in the usual way (cf.
(
DycNeg12
, Lem. 5.1)
) by invoking IH twice: first, IH replaces the eigenvariable of the
(\supset_{r})
,
(\exists_{l})
,
(\forall_{r})
, or
(ihd)
rule with a fresh one, and second, the substitution of
(lsub)
or
(psub)
is performed, after which, the corresponding rule may be applied to derive the desired conclusion.

The
\{(wk),(ctr_{\mathcal{R}}),(ctr_{l}),(ctr_{r})\}
rules.
The hp-admissibility of
(wk)
,
(ctr_{\mathcal{R}})
,
(ctr_{l})
, and
(ctr_{r})
is shown by induction on the height of the given derivation. Hp-admissibility of
(wk)
is relatively straightforward; the only non-trivial cases are the
(\supset_{r})
,
(\exists_{l})
,
(\forall_{r})
, and
(ihd)
rules of the inductive step due to the eigenvariable condition. Such cases are resolved, however, by potentially applying hp-admissibility of
(lsub)
or
(psub)
(argued above), then IH, and last the corresponding rule. Hp-admissibility of
(ctr_{\mathcal{R}})
is simple; any application of the rule to an initial sequent yields an initial sequent, and every case in the inductive step is resolved by applying IH followed by the corresponding rule. The
(ctr_{l})
and
(ctr_{r})
cases are also quite straightforward. The only non-trivial cases occur when a principal occurrence of an
(\supset_{r})
,
(\exists_{l})
, or
(\forall_{r})
rule is contracted. In such cases, the inductive step is solved by invoking the hp-invertibility of each rule (property (iii) below), followed by a potential application of
(lsub)
or
(psub)
, an application of IH, and finally, the hp-admissibility of
(ctr_{\mathcal{R}})
if needed.

Claim (iii).
The cases for the propositional rules are straightforward to check, so we omit them. By hp-admissibility of
(wk)
, we know that
(\exists_{r})
,
(\forall_{l})
,
(ihd)
,
(nd)
, and
(cd)
are hp-invertible (note that the proof of
(wk)
admissibility does not depend on the hp-invertibility of rules holding, so we may invoke it). We therefore only need to check that
(\forall_{r})
and
(\exists_{l})
are hp-invertible. We prove the claim by induction on the height of the given derivation of
\mathcal{R},\Gamma\Rightarrow w:\forall xA,\Delta
for the
(\forall_{r})
rule; the proof for
(\exists_{l})
is similar.

Base case.
If the height of the derivation is
0
, then
\mathcal{R},w\leq v,a\in D_{v},\Gamma\Rightarrow v:A(\underline{a}/x),\Delta
is either an instance of
(\bot_{l})
or
(id_{q})
.

Inductive step.
If the last rule applied in the derivation is
(\wedge_{l})
,
(\wedge_{r})
,
(\vee_{l})
,
(\vee_{r})
,
(\supset_{l})
,
(ref)
,
(tra)
,
(\exists_{r})
,
(\forall_{l})
,
(nd)
, or
(cd)
, then the conclusion follows by applying IH followed by an application of the associated rule. If the last rule applied is
(\supset_{r})
,
(\exists_{l})
,
(\forall_{r})
, or
(ihd)
(where the principal formula of
(\forall_{r})
is in
\Delta
), then we potentially apply hp-admissibility of
(lsub)
or
(psub)
(property (ii) above), followed by IH, and then an application of the corresponding rule. If the last rule applied is
(\forall_{r})
, with
w:\forall xA
the principal formula, then the premise of the inference gives the desired result.

Claim (iv).
We prove the admissibility of
(cut)
by induction on the lexicographic ordering of tuples
(|A|,h_{1},h_{2})
, where
|A|
is the complexity of the cut formula
A
,
h_{1}
is the height of the left premise of
(cut)
, and
h_{2}
is the height of the right premise of
(cut)
. We only consider the cases where the cut formula is principal in both premises of
(cut)
; the other cases where the cut formula is not principal in one premise, or in both premises, are relatively straightforward to verify, though the large number of cases makes the proof tedious. By the cut admissibility theorem for
\mathsf{G3Int}

DycNeg12
, Thm. 5.6)
, we need only verify the cases where the cut formula is of the form
\forall xB
or
\exists xB

Similar to Thm.
3.1
-(i).

By induction on the height of the given derivation—similar to the proofs given for Thm.
3.1
-(ii). Note that the hp-admissibility of
(ctr_{r})
invokes property (iii) below.

Despite this shortcoming, the rules are still invertible. To show this, we prove the following two claims by induction on the height of the given derivation.

(a)

If
\mathcal{R},w_{1}:A\land B,\ldots,w_{n}:A\land B,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta
is provable, then so is the sequent
\mathcal{R},w_{1}:A,w_{1}:B,\ldots,w_{n}:A,w_{n}:B,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta
.

(b)

If
\mathcal{R},w_{1}:\exists xA,\ldots,w_{n}:\exists xA,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta
is provable, then so is the sequent
\mathcal{R},\underline{a}_{1}\in D_{w_{1}},\ldots,\underline{a}_{n}\in D_{w_{n}},w_{1}:A(\underline{a}_{1}/x),\ldots,w_{n}:A(\underline{a}_{n}/x),\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta
.

Claim (a).
The base case is trivial, so we move on to the inductive step.

Inductive step.
Excluding the case of
(lift)
, the result follows by applying IH followed by the relevant rule, or in the case where one of the conjunction formulae is principal in a
(\wedge_{r})
inference, apply IH to the premise (if needed) to obtain the desired result. If none of the conjunctions are active in a
(lift)
inference, then apply IH followed by an application of
(lift)
. If one of the conjunctions is principal in an application of
(lift)
(as shown below top), then resolve the case as shown below bottom; we assume w.l.o.g. that the label of the principal formula is
w_{1}
.

\mathcal{R},u\leq w_{1},u:A\land B,w_{1}:A\land B,\ldots,w_{n}:A\land B,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

(lift)

\mathcal{R},u\leq w_{1},u:A\land B,\ldots,w_{n}:A\land B,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

IH

\mathcal{R},u\leq w_{1},u:A,u:B,w_{1}:A,w_{1}:B,\ldots,w_{n}:A,w_{n}:B,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

(lift)

\mathcal{R},u\leq w_{1},u:A,u:B,w_{1}:B,\ldots,w_{n}:A,w_{n}:B,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

(lift)

\mathcal{R},u\leq w_{1},u:A,u:B,\ldots,w_{n}:A,w_{n}:B,\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

Notice that the two applications of

needed to derive the desired conclusion break the hp-invertibility of the
(\wedge_{l})
rule.

Claim (b).
The base case is trivial, so we move on to the inductive step.

Inductive step.
All cases, with the exception of the one given below top (where one of our existential formulae is principal in an application of
(lift)
), are either resolved by applying IH followed by the corresponding rule, or if one of the existential formulae is principal in an
(\exists_{r})
inference, then apply IH to the premise (if needed) to obtain the desired result. The non-trivial case given below top is resolved as shown below bottom; we assume w.l.o.g. that the label of the principal formula is
w_{1}

Lemma
15
.

The
(ref)
and
(tra)
rules are admissible in the calculus
\mathsf{G3IntQC}^{*}
.

Proof

We prove the result by induction on the height of the given derivation. We assume w.l.o.g. that the last inference in the given derivation is an instance of
(ref)
or
(tra)
, and that this is the only instance of the rule in the given derivation. The general result follows by successively eliminating topmost occurrences of
(ref)
or
(tra)
from a given derivation until it is free of such inferences. By Lem.
5
and Lem.
16
, we need only consider the non-trivial
(id^{c}_{q})
,
(\exists^{c}_{r})
,
(\exists^{ic}_{r})
,
(\forall^{c}_{l})
,
(\forall^{ic}_{l})
,
(nd)
, and
(cd)
cases.

Base case.
We let
\mathcal{R}^{\prime}:=\mathcal{R},\underline{a}_{1}\in D_{v_{1}},\ldots,\underline{a}_{n}\in D_{v_{n}}
in the
(id^{n}_{q})
cases below. In both the
(ref)
and
(tra)
cases, the side condition that there is an undirected path from
v_{i}
to
w
, for each
i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}
, holds in the end sequent. If none of the undirected paths from
v_{i}
to
w
contain
u\leq u
(
u\leq z^{\prime}
), then the paths are present in
\mathcal{R}^{\prime}
(
\mathcal{R}^{\prime},u\leq z,z\leq z^{\prime}
, resp.), and if an undirected path from
v_{i}
to
w
contains
u\leq u
(
u\leq z^{\prime}
, resp.), then deleting each occurrence of
u\leq u
from the undirected path (replacing each occurrence of
u\leq z^{\prime}
with
u\leq z,z\leq z^{\prime}
, resp.) gives a new path from
v_{i}
to
w
.

(cd)

(cd)

\mathcal{R},w\leq u,u\leq v,a\in D_{v},\Gamma\Rightarrow\Delta

We now argue that the side condition
v\sim^{\mathcal{R}}w
of
(\exists^{c}_{r})
,
(\exists^{ic}_{r})
,
(\forall^{c}_{l})
, and
(\forall^{ic}_{l})
continues to hold after applying IH. If the undirected path from
v
to
w
does not contain
u\leq z^{\prime}
, then the side condition trivially holds. If, on the other hand, the undirected path from
v
to
w
contains
u\leq z^{\prime}
, then another undirected path from
v
to
w
is found by replacing all occurrences of
u\leq z^{\prime}
with
u\leq z,z\leq z^{\prime}
, which continues to be present after the invocation of IH.
∎
